#3415. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

Now that we know that a Red Rising movie is in the works, it's completely understandable that we'd be on the edges of our seats waiting for any word on who might be cast in the book-to-screen adaptation. Eagle-eyed Red Rising fans -- yes, that's an intentional nod to the Bellona sigil right there -- have picked up on the fact that author Pierce Brown has followed Joseph Zada on Instagram, which has led to a lot of enthusiastic speculation that the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping star might be in talks to play a role in Red Rising movie. I've seen one specific character name coming up a lot as the perfect role for Zada to take on, but wait a second, because there are options here.

To be clear up front, there is no official word that Zada is in talks to star in the Red Rising movie. However, it's not a stretch that his name would be circulating. As mentioned, fans noticed Pierce Brown followed Zada on Instagram. Then there's the fact that Zada is currently starring in Francis Lawrence's most recent movie adaptation. Given the news that Lawrence will be directing the Red Rising movie, it stands to reason that he might be considering people he's worked with already for the cast.

On the other hand, the fact that Pierce Brown and Francis Lawrence have known each other for years (per Lawrence) also needs to be acknowledged, as Brown could've met Zada through the director and followed him just to follow him... as people do. In short, the follow could mean nothing or it could mean something.

However, since we're speculating, I want to talk about the role(s) he'd be right to take, starting with the one that seems to be a crowd favorite.

The handsome Bellona's name came up quite a bit in the comments discussing who Zada should play, and I get it. Even as Golds go, Cassius is known to be extremely handsome, and well, Zada fits that description. Zada's also got the blond curls, which is one of the most distinctive things about Cassius' looks. Also, as a Gold, Cassius is tall, and so is Zada.

When it comes to casting the Gold characters (and Obsidians) in the movie, it seems unlikely that they're going to find the perfect actors to play the roles, who also just so happen to be around or above seven feet tall. How they make the size differences among the colors stand out on screen is going to be a challenge by itself, whether they use forced perspective, special effects or other techniques. Still, if they want to cast actors on the taller side for the Golds, IMDB has Zada listed as 6'2".

Relative to men of average height, Zada's reported height (or anywhere in the ballpark of six feet, really) seems like a good fit for a Gold on screen. That brings me to the alternate speculation, because I don't think Cassius is the only option, or possibly even the best one.

Darrow's the other name I've seen circulating, and honestly, he's the first person I thought of when I saw the topic of Joseph Zada possibly starring in the Red Rising movie. Maybe it's seeing him play a District 12 kid in Sunrise on the Reaping that makes it easier for me to envision him as a lowRed with a score to settle. There are a lot of sides to Darrow, especially when we factor in the teen that he is at the start of Red Rising, and the transition (and drama) he goes through in the first book. I can see Zada tackling that arc really well.

Nah. I can't even picture it... but it'd be fun to see his take on the role.

I'm going to cross Pax off the list right away. Even if Zada bulked up a lot for the part, I picture a guy with the size and personality of a jovial (or ferocious, when necessary) bear for the youngest Telemanus son. However, Roque would be an interesting option. I don't think Zada fits how I imagine Roque to look, but I do think he'd have an interesting take on the thoughtful character.

The last person I considered was The Jackal. While his role in the first book is fairly limited -- he's present more by reputation than he actually is on page -- he does get one of the most memorable scenes, and after playing the hero in the Hunger Games movie, I really wouldn't mind seeing what Zada does with a dark and twisty character like The Jackal.

Whether or not Zada gets cast in the Red Rising movie remains to be seen, but he does seem like a great candidate for a role, and from what he told Xtra, it sounds like he's interested in being involved.

#3413. If You're Tired Of Colleen Hoover Movies, Watch This Overlooked 2026 Rom-Com

Colleen Hoover is the reigning queen of BookTok-phenomenon-turned-movie entertainment. The woman just has a knack for writing the kinds of books that might not get a lot of critical love but which social media crowds cannot resist. Thus far, that has resulted in four Colleen Hoover movie adaptations. Unfortunately, none of them are very good. At least, the critics didn't like them. Audiences, on the other hand, keep showing up. Following the less than enthusiastic response to the latest Hoover movie, "Verity," however, even fans might be in need of a break. In which case, might I suggest "You, Me & Tuscany," directed by Kat Coiro.

Corio previously helmed the 2022 glossy rom-com relic "Marry Me" starring Jennifer Lopez and Owen Wilson. Like your standard Hoover affair, it movie earned an okay 61% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, but managed to push the "popcornmeter" to 92%, meaning audiences absolutely loved Coiro's movie — which was based on a webcomic.

In 2026, Coiro — who also directed several episodes of "She-Hulk: Attorney at Law" — returned with another romantic comedy: "You, Me & Tuscany," an original story written by Ryan Engle, who, oddly enough, has mostly written actioners such as the Idris-Elba-vs.-a-lion survival horror "Beast" and the Liam Neeson outing that was 2014's "Non-Stop." With "You, Me & Tuscany" he embraced his more tender side with a story of a young cook who finds love in the titular Italian region.

"You, Me & Tuscany" stars Halle Bailey ("The Little Mermaid") as Anna, a young woman who after losing her house-sitting job, meets a strapping Italian named Matteo Costa (Lorenzo de Moor). Following their brief encounter, Anna decides to fly to Italy and manages to find a spare key to Matteo's empty Tuscan villa. There, Matteo's mother, Gabriella (Isabella Ferrari) arrives and Anna decides to lie and tell her that she's Matteo's fiancé.

It might seem as though "You, Me & Tuscany" is yet another fake dating rom-com, whereby a feigned romance becomes real. But the movie diverges from that well-worn path when Matteo's cousin, Michael (Regé-Jean Page) arrives and there's an instant attraction between he and Anna.

Page is, of course, best known for playing Simon Basset, the Duke of Hastings, in Season 1 of Netflix's hugely-popular series "Bridgerton." But he's since enjoyed a successful film career and is quickly making a name for himself in Hollywood. Page's Simon Basset left "Bridgerton" after the first season, after which the actor appeared in "Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves," and in Steven Soderbergh's sleek spy thriller "Black Bag." With "You, Me & Tuscany" he further proved he has leading man chops. Otherwise, however, the movie doesn't do much to separate it from the glut of sort-of-okay romance movies with which we've been inundated in recent years. But it has at least outdone every Colleen Hoover movie on Rotten Tomatoes.

The latest Colleen Hoover movie was the dead-on-arrival "Verity," which no doubt left many viewers disappointed in the lack of straightforward romance. Much of the movie features Anne Hathaway glaring silently at Dakota Johnson from a medical bed or wheelchair. "You, Me and Tuscany" on the other hand should delight those hoping for more schmaltzy romance in the vein of Lili Reinhart's Prime Video smash hit "The Love Hypothesis" or Sofia Carson's similarly popular Netflix romance "My Oxford Year."

Over on Rotten Tomatoes, it's a familiar state of affairs. "You, Me & Tuscany" earned a somewhat respectable 65% critic score while managing to push the "popcornmeter" all the way to 91%. This is the rom-com pattern of late. Audiences clearly got what they came for here, even if Nikki Gemmell of The Australian called the movie "the filmic equivalent of paint by numbers, lift muzak, Fruit Loops, Contiki Tours and The Voice," essentially "anything that feels bland, inauthentic and deeply commercial." Sadly, this is just where we are in 2026. We used to make rom-coms like "Sleepless in Seattle" and "When Harry Met Sally." Not anymore.

"You, Me & Tuscany," however, isn't the worst example of the modern day rom-com (Netflix's "The Wrong Paris" might have claimed that title in 2025). If you happen to be looking for a Hoover palette cleanser that also isn't too far removed from the author's BookTok-friendly brand of romance, then this one's worth a go. "You, Me & Tuscany" is currently available to rent from the usual platforms, and can be streamed via Peacock with a premium subscription.

#3412. The One Thing to Know About Jason and Lucia Before You Play Too Much GTA 6

GTA 6 is at its best when Jason and Lucia are together

Even after clearing Grand Theft Auto 6’s long story, I keep finding myself drawn back to Leonida. That’s thanks in large part to Jason and Lucia, a pair of charismatic protagonists that I genuinely enjoy spending time with. While you can treat them as independent characters and take them out on solo adventures, GTA 6 shines brightest when you travel around Leonida as a pair. In fact, you’re bound to miss a whole lot if you aren’t letting Jason and Lucia enjoy a date from time to time.

While playing as one character in GTA 6, you have the option to invite your partner to hang out with you. (This feature unlocks partway through Chapter 2 of the story.) If you’re playing as Jason, for instance, you could text Lucia and ask if she wants to hang out, prompting her to drive to your location. You can coordinate crimes this way too; if you find a bank you want to rob, you can ping Jason and tell him to meet Lucia at the spot to pull off the job together. There are a lot of benefits to working together, as heists will become easier and you’ll be able to ask your partner to run off and fence any goods you grab.

But keeping Jason and Lucia together has some less obvious benefits, too. When the two explore together, they’ll occasionally break out into natural conversations. One time while driving through Lummox County listening to a country radio station, Lucia talked about how she thought the genre was a joke growing up. A little odd couple exchange ensued, where Jason talked about how much he loves country music. Later, upon finding a stray bicycle, Lucia told Jason about the time she tried to ride a bike as a kid and crashed into an ice cream truck.

There are even entire running gags that you’ll only hear while playing together. One recurring bit involves Lucia constantly answering spam robocalls and gradually losing her cool over them. That culminates in her giving the AI voice a firm thrashing, while Jason chuckles from the sidelines. Those bits of contextual chatter help make Jason and Lucia feel like an authentic couple rather than voiceless pawns to be moved around.

More importantly, crucial story details can come out of those moments. One time while exploring a swamp in search of Skunk Ape effigies (weird game!), Jason and Lucia broke out into a conversation about their family dynamics. It started when Jason mentioned Lucia’s mother doesn’t like him very much. After a bit of unconvincing denial, Lucia admitted that there’s truth to Jason’s anxiety: Lucia lied to her mother, saying that Jason essentially walked out on her and their child. That revelation triggered a conversation where Lucia recalled a moment where Jason once told her he didn’t want children, which is why she initially didn’t tell Jason about their son. It’s an important moment that gives depth to Jason and Lucia’s history and fills in some questions about why Tommy was kept secret for so long.

So, if you’ve been exploring Leonida solo for most of your GTA 6 playthrough, make sure to invite your partner to hang out regularly. You’ll miss some of the best human moments in the game if you do, and you’ll understand each character so much more by listening to their chatter. And, of course, you’ll also be able to send Jason off with a bag full of cocaine if you don’t want to trek back to Vice City to sell it.

#3410. Leighton Meester's Christmas Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

Former "Gossip Girl" star Leighton Meester is currently dominating the Netflix streaming charts with her latest movie. A now-famous actress whose career started on "Law & Order," she's come a long way over the years. To that end, Meester's "Guarding Stars" is now the biggest streaming hit on the biggest streaming service in the world.

Described as "a cozy, snowy Christmas rom-com," director Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum's "Guarding Stars" is currently sitting in the number one spot on Netflix's most-watched movie charts, per FlixPatrol. The movie co-stars former "Supernatural" star Jared Padalecki. Since The CW canceled Padelecki's "Walker," he's had more time to focus on other stuff, such as this holiday flavored romantic comedy.

The movie centers on a no-nonsense bodyguard (Meester) who is assigned to protect a charming action star over the holidays. Sparks fly, secrets unravel, and Christmas gets a whole lot more complicated. The movie is inspired by the 2022 novel "The Bodyguard" by Katherine Center. The ensemble cast also includes Andie MacDowell ("Magic Mike XXL"), Noah LaLonde ("Deer Camp '86"), Toby Sandeman ("Running Point"), Rachael Ancheril ("Star Trek: Discovery"), Shaun Johnston ("Heartland"), pop star Ava Max, and country singer Walker Hayes in his acting debut.

Netflix wisely decided to drop this movie just before Thanksgiving. The holidays are kicking off and this is very much on point with the theme of the holiday. It's precisely the kind of thing people are looking to throw on while scrolling for something to watch. This sort of stuff thrives this time of year. As further evidence of that, the Colleen Hoover movie "Reminders of Him" was also recently Netflix's biggest streaming hit.

Rom-coms can still find success at the box office these days, with Glen Powell and Sydney Sweeney's "Anyone But You" serving as a fine example from recent history. But Netflix has really managed to dominate this space in recent years. They've made genuinely charming gems like "Always Be My Maybe," one of the best rom-coms on Netflix, and launched full-on franchises such as "The Kissing Booth."

But the king of the streamers has really thrived when it comes to romantic holiday fare. One of the most prominent examples was when 2024's strange Christmas movie "Hot Frosty" took over Netflix, becoming a genuine cultural sensation at the time. Admittedly, "Guarding Stars" is much more traditional than a movie in which a snowman comes to life. All the same, that almost makes its success more noteworthy, as it didn't have to rely on some goofy hook to get it across the finish line.

There's probably an element of this premise that seems cozy and fitting the spirit of the season, but pairing two former CW stars like Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki, especially with one in an against-type role as a bodyguard, appears to have intrigued viewers quite a bit.

The movie was written by Erin Cardillo and Richard Keith ("Isn't It Romantic," "Virgin River") alongside Gina Matthews and Grant Scharbo. Robin Fisichella served as the executive producer, with Matthews, Scharbo, Jared and Genevieve Padalecki on board as producers.

"Guarding Stars" is streaming now on Netflix.

Sylvester Stallone shares an idea for a new Taylor Sheridan series starring his former box office rival turned friend, Arnold Schwarzenegger.

Best known as Rocky and Rambo, Stallone's first leading role in a television series came in 2022, starring in Taylor Sheridan's Tulsa King as Dwight "The General" Manfredi, a New York mafia capo who, after serving a 25-year prison sentence, is exiled to Oklahoma to set up his own criminal organization. The series has been a hit, with Tulsa King season 4 currently airing new episodes on Paramount+.

Now, in Cigar Aficionado's new cover story, Sylvester Stallone says he wants Arnold Schwarzenegger to star in a Tulsa King spinoff, with their characters eventually crossing paths, much like they did in The Expendables franchise. Read his full comments below:

I would love in a perfect world to do an extension of Tulsa King starring [Schwarzenegger] in his own show. Since we’re comrades in the fantasy world, our characters meet and discuss things, like we did in The Expendables. I hope he agrees.

No such spinoff has officially been announced or entered development, so Stallone may simply be testing the idea publicly. When The Hollywood Reporter reached out, Paramount+ and producer 101 Studios had no immediate comment.

Stallone and Schwarzenegger have shared the silver screen four times, including in three Expendables movies (2010–2014) and the prison-set action thriller Escape Plan (2013). From the late 1970s to the 1990s, the two action stars engaged in a bitter rivalry, frequently competing with each other at the box office. By the late 1990s, they built bridges, leading to a lasting friendship.

Tulsa King already has one upcoming spinoff, Frisco King, starring Samuel L. Jackson as Russell Lee Washington Jr., who made his debut in Tulsa King season 3. Premiering on December 18, the spinoff follows Russell Washington as he relocates to Texas to build his own criminal enterprise. Stallone's Dwight Manfredi will appear in the first episode of Frisco King, but is not expected to have a regular role beyond that.

If Stallone gets his wish, the question will become where Schwarzenegger's character would establish his own criminal empire. While Las Vegas, Atlantic City, or Detroit are intriguing possibilities, both Tulsa King and Frisco King are set in what are seen as untapped criminal markets in the Southwest.

Of course, all of this remains wishful thinking for now, as it's unclear whether Schwarzenegger is even interested in taking on a Tulsa King spinoff. Still, the prospect of reuniting the two action legends in Sheridan's expanding crime universe is certainly intriguing. For now, fans can only hope Stallone's pitch receives a positive response.

#3408. Stranger Things Star Noah Schnapp Reveals Photo From Failed Hunger Games Audition For Haymitch

Now that he's free of "Stranger Things," we're going to find out if Noah Schnapp can fulfill the promise he flashed over five seasons of the Netflix sci-fi/horror series. His character, Will Byers, had arguably the most emotional arc of the show, with viewers watching him go from missing boy to psychically tortured returnee from the Upside Down to out and proud young adult. Byers' journey mirrored Schnapp's personal voyage to coming out of the closet in 2025. It was a lovely moment for Schnapp, both as an individual and also for his character, who presented a positive gay role model for kids who too often struggle with prejudice and outright hatred in their everyday lives.

I've no idea if Schnapp will return to the "Stranger Things" universe (he's only just portrayed a disaffected rich kid and, when the plot jumps forward 20 years, the kid's son in Andy Sandberg's controversial stage play "Affluenza"), but he had a shot at joining the "Hunger Games" franchise as a young Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." The "Hunger Games" prequel is currently tearing up the box office, so it would've been a sweet gig for the 22-year-old actor. But he congratulated Joseph Zada like a gentleman for landing the role, and, as an egoless bonus, the brunette Schnapp posted a still picture of himself in blonde hair from his screen test to Instagram. (See below.)

After a couple of ... emojis, Schnapp tagged Zada and added, "Think they picked right for this one."

I have no true measure of Noah Schnapp as an actor. He's handsome, he's got some mystery to him and, in the right role (e.g. Will Byers), he connects. Do I think he would've been an effective Haymitch Abernathy, given all the horrible things that happen to the character on his way to growing up and becoming Woody Harrelson? Maybe not.

"Affluenza" ended its London run on November 21, and, boy, did the critics lay into this sucker. In a one-star review for The Guardian, Arifa Akbar called it an "epic wreckage," adding, "You want to look away, for shame, but simply can't stop gawping." Most critics concurred, but that actually worked out for Schnapp, as they were too busy lambasting Sandberg to pay much attention to his performance. Writing for The Times, Clive Davis simply noted that Schnapp "doesn't disgrace himself." If you get cast in a disaster, you can live with that.

It's unclear where Schnapp will go from here, but thanks to "Stranger Things" he has a pretty sizable fan base. I can't see him being a part of the forthcoming series "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure," which is a prequel set in the 1950s, but we'll certainly see more of him in the future.

#3405. This X-Men Character Is The One Marvel Hero Doctor Doom Respects The Most

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Doctor Victor von Doom's ego and conviction in his own superiority are as enormous as the universe, but in his cold heart, he does respect some of the "foolish" heroes who oppose him. Doom unconditionally loves his goddaughter, Valeria Richards of the Fantastic Four. He is frenemies with Namor the Sub-Mariner, and also maintains a friendly rivalry with his fellow sorcerer Doctor Stephen Strange; their dynamic lacks the bitterness that defines Doom's feud with Reed Richards. Doom also acknowledges Captain America as a paragon of his chosen ideals, and sees even Spider-Man's puerility as if he's a court jester, the one willing to tell a king what no one else will.

But there's one hero that Doom most consistently views and addresses as an equal, and that's Ororo Monroe, Storm, of the X-Men. Storm is easily one of the strongest X-Men; she can control the weather itself and is a self-styled "goddess." Even Doom concedes her that description. Unusually for Doom, he rarely tries to downplay Storm's power next to his own. Ororo's strength intrigues him — as does her beauty.

Now, Doom isn't the kind of man to act on romantic whimsy. "Doom needs no one" is one of his self-affirming catchphrases, and he once drove away his childhood sweetheart Valeria to prioritize his quest for knowledge and power. Part of Doom's self-inflicted misery is choosing to believe that no woman could ever love a man with a scarred face like his, yet another reason Doom hides behind a mask: "How could she... when even I am driven to madness by the sight!" But even so, one feels Doom would revel in the fantasy of Storm sitting by his side. It all goes back to their first meeting in "Uncanny X-Men" #145 by Chris Claremont and Dave Cockrum.

"Uncanny X-Men" issues #145-147 comprise a short arc where the twisted gamesman Arcade teams up with Doom to destroy the X-Men. In #145, Storm shows up at Doom's castle... and he welcomes her as an honored guest, treating her to a feast while the other X-Men are attacked by mecha-armored guards. Storm herself is charmed by Doom, thinking he is "a fascinating man," and he reciprocates.

"Storm seems drawn to me, as I am to her. Lioness to lion. Queen to king. She does not fear me. She should. She will."

Indeed, Doom soon defeats the X-Men, Storm included, as he dismisses them all as simple "children" next to him. While the others are thrown into deathtraps, Doom — charmed as he was by Storm — transmutes the still conscious Ororo into a chrome statue, while creating a robot in Storm's image to serve him. For Ororo, who is claustrophobic, being trapped inside her own body is a living hell. Once freed, she lives up to her name and unfurls a terrifying storm. Echoing Doom's own words, Storm declares: "Am I not beautiful, Lord Doom? And terrible? Do you not fear me? You should. You shall."

Normally, this would be a bungled first impression. But after surrendering Arcade, Doom apologizes to Storm for his behavior, suggesting his infatuation with her was real: "I would hope that we might begin anew. You are a fascinating woman. I should like to know you better." Ororo grants him the grace of a clean slate.

The events of this arc are referenced almost any time Doom and Storm meet, such as in issue #4 of Storm's 2024 solo series, where Doom hosts her in Latveria. He's not alone among villains in his view of Storm, either.

Read any of Chris Claremont's writing, including the hundreds of "X-Men" stories to his name, and it's easy to tell that he's got a thing for powerful women. No "X-Men" character more consistently shows that than Storm, the strongest of the team and their frequent leader. It often feels like Claremont wrote his own infatuation with the character into the text; "powerful villain tries to take Storm as theirs" is a stock Claremont "X-Men" plot, and not just with Doom.

Claremont and Bill Sienkiewicz's "Uncanny X-Men" #159 sees Dracula himself try to turn Storm into his bride. (New comic series "Midnight X-Men" takes place in a timeline where he succeeded, and Storm reigns as a vampire queen.)

An attraction to Storm binds Doom and Dracula... or does it? Shortly after Doom's guest appearance in "X-Men," writer-artist John Byrne took over "Fantastic Four." Byrne had made his name drawing "X-Men," but ultimately left due to creative differences with Claremont. A lingering mark of those differences shows up in "Fantastic Four" #258. Byrne, apparently dissatisfied with how Claremont wrote Doom, suggests the Doom who teamed up with Arcade was one of Doom's robotic duplicates, or Doombots.

Now, in the "X-Men" issues themselves, there's no hint this isn't the real Doom. Years later, in Al Ewing and Stefano Caselli's "S.W.O.R.D." #7, Storm hosts Doom for dinner, and their conversation is loaded with references to "X-Men" #145. Doom blames his unbecoming behavior of attacking Storm, his guest, as a Doombot's faulty programming (but he would, wouldn't he?). Across the conversation, Doom demonstrates his interest in Storm is all too real, to the point Ororo tells him: "Don't flirt, Victor. It's unbecoming." Except, Doom would likely argue, with an exceptional woman like her.

#3404. The Witcher 4 Will Be a GTA 6-Sized Leap Forward, CD Projekt Red Says

CDPR addresses comparisons between its games and Grand Theft Auto 6

We're living in a post-Grand Theft Auto 6 world now, meaning that almost every other game in development will inevitably be compared to Rockstar Games' new open-world crime drama. The developer behind two other big open-world brands, The Witcher and Cyberpunk, is now fielding questions about how its future games will stack up against GTA 6.

During an earnings call on Tuesday, CD Projekt Red joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski addressed the Leonida-sized elephant in the room: how GTA 6 will influence his company's upcoming games, The Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2. Nowakowski said that he believes The Witcher 4 will deliver a GTA 6-like leap forward for players.

"Of course, we did look at the game," Nowakowski said of GTA 6, adding, "We did see the differences" between it and 2013's Grand Theft Auto 5. "We believe there's going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4. It's been 11 years. We are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game. So, yes, you should expect us to make a much, much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4."

"We have certain ambitions when it comes to [The Witcher 4] and Cyberpunk 2," he said. "They have not changed when it comes to GTA 6. If anything happened as a result of GTA 6, it's [that it's] always great to see games like that because they show you how much cool stuff can be done, and that's for sure an inspiration in many ways for our developers."

Nowakowski also addressed The Witcher 4's through the lens of GTA 6's budget. Rockstar's latest release is rumored to have a development budget of more than $1 billion, and Nowakowski categorized CD Projekt Red's upcoming games as not having "budget-driven developments."

"I'm not saying we don't care about the budgets. We do," he said. "I'm pretty sure [Rockstar] did as well. But you cannot make games like that having in mind This is the fixed number of money I want to spend and that's it, otherwise we’re gone. They're ambition-driven developments and money's important. The budgets are not indefinite, that's not what we're saying. And honestly that philosophy has not changed for us because of GTA 6's release; it has just always been like that."

As for other lessons learned from GTA 6's massive launch, Nowakowski noted that "If you want to reach a certain critical mass, you do have to get out of the core main gaming bubble, [which is] something we did achieve in the past as well. Our games are different and they require a certain different approach. But in terms of the ultimate effect in terms of breaking out to the mass market, awareness, this is something we consider critical."

In other words, while CD Projekt Red may take some cues from Rockstar Games, it's not trying to copy the Grand Theft Auto developer's homework.

The Witcher 4 is slated for release in 2028. Cyberpunk 2 does not have an announced release window.

#3403. Why There Are No New NCIS, New York, & Origins Tonight (Nov 24) & When They Return For Fresh Episodes

Tuesday nights are one of the best nights for TV. It means the NCIS trio takes pride of place on the small screen, and there's certainly a lot of excitement as the shows get ready for their winter breaks. It was just last year when CBS finally put NCIS back in its rightful place, kicking off Tuesdays in style, and it was joined by two other shows.

While there has been a small change with NCIS: Sydney not returning in the fall, the new spinoff NCIS: New York has more than made up for it. LL Cool J and Scott Caan's refreshing change has brought an energy to the screen that hasn't been seen in a few years, and the rest of the team brings mystery, intrigue, and humor. Sure, there is some disappointment in that NCIS: Origins season 3 will only have 10 episodes, but each of those installments features Mark Harmon as Gibbs once more, bringing much-needed answers about Lala and a new mystery to unravel.

As for the flagship series, NCIS season 24 has gained one thing that was missing: Tony DiNozzo. Michael Weatherly's return has proven DiNozzo was the missing piece on NCIS for the longest time, while delivering a mature man worthy of the director's chair. With all this, there is the understandable question about why there are no new episodes of the NCIS universe on CBS tonight.

After just taking a week off due to the midterm elections, the NCIS franchise barely gives anyone time to recover as it takes another break. This time it's linked to Thanksgiving, as CBS has opted to give almost all shows on the schedule a break. Usually, Thursday and Friday shows are preempted because of Thanksgiving itself, and it's become expected since people want to gather with family or friends, and they're more likely to put the football on.

Taking a break earlier in the week hasn't been as common in the past. While the NCIS shows took time off in 2025, they didn't in 2024. However, as viewership has declined over the years, it makes sense to preempt most shows as people get ready to spend time with family, with some traveling during Thanksgiving Eve or earlier to beat the holiday rush.

Instead of airing new episodes, CBS will still have a night of NCIS, packing the November 24 schedule with reruns. It all starts with a rerun of the NCIS season 23 episode titled "Her," which saw the return of Ellie Bishop, finally offering closure for viewers and Torres. After that, the pilot episode of NCIS: New York will air, offering those who may have missed it a chance to see LL Cool J's newest series introduction.

While NCIS: Origins usually airs in the final slot of the night, that's not happening tonight. Unfortunately, CBS has opted for another NCIS rerun instead, airing another NCIS season 23 episode, titled "Fleeting." This brought far more trouble to Fleet Week than normal, with a sailor turning up dead in the trunk of a car.

While the break is disappointing, there is some good news. The break is not a long one, with all three NCIS shows set to return on December 1, 2026, with all-new episodes on CBS. Don't forget there's also a chance to watch whichever NCIS episode you want on Paramount+.

In even better news, these episodes won't be the fall finales. While NBC and ABC have opted to bring many of their shows to a close before Thanksgiving, CBS will continue to air new episodes later into December. NCIS, New York, and Origins will all air their fall finales on December 8, 2026, and even the winter hiatus isn't going to be that long.

When NCIS season 24 returns, it will be with an episode titled "Lucky Shot." MCRT is pulled into a case that involves a freelance nightcrawler videographer who turns up dead. It's soon clear that he was murdered, and the motive is linked to evidence he secretly recorded connected to a cover-up. Not only will the team need to figure out who the murderer is, but they'll also need to uncover a conspiracy that brings danger at every turn.

NCIS: New York will deliver its seventh hour of the season, titled "The River." Like other episodes in the new LL Cool J series, this one won't necessarily involve a murder. It could turn out that way, but the team is called in when a Marine sergeant's car is discovered after he fled Quantico. This Marine sergeant was supposed to be going on a high-stakes mission, and now the question is whether he left on his own accord or if something more serious is going on.

Although it was a gamble, the NCIS franchise taking a risk with its future is already paying off for CBS as its newest series continues to roll out.

In the final hour of the night, NCIS: Origins returns with en episode titled "Don't Let the Day Go By." This is a huge hour in the present day, as Gibbs turns to another former colleague and friend, Vera. Roma Maffia returns to the universe once more, reprising her role as Vera Strickland, to help Gibbs get to the bottom of those who are after him. Of course, he now needs to figure out what really happened to Lala, and why she wasn't on that plane.

In the past, the team would need to deal with the murder of a Marine. This is far more than a traditional murder, though, as the Marine is missing a tongue, and that usually means some sort of mob or cartel is involved. In this case, the team will come face to face with a Russian serial killer.

The fall finales of all three NCIS universe shows will air on December 8, 2026. It will then be time for the winter hiatus, but get ready for all three shows to be back before January comes to an end. CBS has set the date as January 12, 2027.

#3402. The Best Tech Deals From Costco's Early Black Friday Sale

Sam's Club, Walmart, Amazon, and other retailers have been churning out early Black Friday deals since last week, so if you haven't been paying attention, you've already missed out on some good deals. But all hope is not lost: Costco recently started its own early sale, so you're still in time to find something you want at a low price. Below, I've rounded up my favorite tech deals from their sale—but keep in mind you'll need a membership to take advantage of these deals.

A powerful monitor with high-end specs can make gaming more immersive and greatly reduce input lag, which is helpful for any serious gamer looking for an edge over their opponents. The Samsung Odyssey G9 is a 49-inch gaming monitor with some impressive specs, including a 240Hz refresh rate and a 1 ms response time. It's available for $699.99 (originally $899.99), $200 off and the lowest price it has reached this year.

If you're looking for a more premium (and far more massive) gaming monitor, the 57-inch Samsung Odyssey Neo G9, one of the best ultra-wide gaming monitors on the market, is currently on sale for $1,449.99 ($2,499.99 at launch). This monitor came out in 2023, earning an "excellent" review from PCMag for its impressive 7,680 x 2,160 4K resolution, its great color range and accuracy, a 240Hz refresh rate, 1,000 nits of brightness, and its overall design. To make full use of its powerful 240Hz refresh rate, you'll need to use DisplayPort 2.1, or you'll be limited to 120Hz. You'll also need a powerful graphics card. But if you have the right setup, this thing really delivers.

The 15.3-inch Lenovo Legion is a powerful gaming laptop with premium specs, and with the current $600 discount, it's down to $1999.99 (originally $2,599.99). It has a powerful AMD Ryzen AI 9 processor, 32 GB of RAM, a GeForce RTX 5070 graphics card, and 1TB of SSD. PCMag gave the more affordable 5i version an excellent review for its price and performance, so if you have the cash for it, this one is even better.

This 5.1 TCL Q6CH setup is currently $199.99 (originally $299.99), including a soundbar and subwoofer. This soundbar came out in 2024 and supports Dolby Atmos and DTS:X for that 3D sound, as well as AI Sonic, a tool that tunes your sound settings based on the setup of your room.

The latest AirPods Pro are a big step up from their previous generation. The third iteration of Apple's iconic earbuds deliver a number of quality-of-life and software improvements that make them worth the typical premium over the AirPods Pro 2—and right now, the AirPods Pro 3 are even cheaper than the previous generation: They're $179 at Costco (originally $249) in an early Black Friday deal.

The 15-inch MacBook Air is down to $1,249 (originally $1,499), the lowest price since Apple hiked prices this past summer. The M5 MacBook Air is the best laptop for most people looking for a new machine in 2026. In comparison to the already excellent M4 Air, the M5 base model has double the storage, and the powerful M5 chip makes the performance even smoother, according to Mashable's review. The aluminum design is as good as you'd expect from Apple's most popular portable laptop, and it includes a Liquid Retina display, Touch ID, a 12MP Center Stage Camera, and the Magic Keyboard.

The 15.6-inch Acer Aspire Go is a great value at its current $499.99 price (originally $699.99). The display is a touchscreen; it sports an AMD Ryzen 5 processor and it has 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. These aren't specs you normally find at this price, making it a great laptop for anyone looking to stretch their money as far as possible while getting a workhorse of a laptop.

I'm a fan of TCL TVs, and currently own the "non-pro" version of this TV. The 65-inch QM6K Pro is $599.99 (originally $999.99) and has the same internal hardware and Mini-LED panel as the regular QM6K, but it adds a CrystGlow anti-reflective coating that makes it more viewable in well-lit rooms and helps maintain a high picture contrast. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

#3401. Guy Pearce's Gory '90s Horror Western Movie Deserved Better At The Box Office

One of the enduring American monster myths is the Wendigo or the forest spirit that possesses and compels men to become cannibals. Originally a myth of the Algonquian peoples, the Wendigo has become a monster of comic books, horror films, and more, like Stephen King's chilling novel "Pet Sematary."

Possibly the strangest Wendigo movie is the 1999 horror western comedy "Ravenous," inspired by real tales of 19th century cannibalism on the frontier like the Donner Party. During the Mexican–American War, Lieutenant John Boyd (Guy Pearce) plays dead during battle. Hidden among a cart of deceased soldiers, Boyd takes an enemy fort. A hero but also a coward, Boyd is then reassigned to a remote outpost in the Sierra Nevada mountains.

Curiously, during Boyd's seizure of the fort, he seemed to gain strength when the blood of the dead dripped down onto his tongue. In that moment, Boyd became an unknowing Wendigo, acquiring the strength of the men whose blood he drank — and he's not the only one on the mountain. A traveler named F.W. Colqhoun (Robert Carlyle) shows up at the fort, claiming to be the survivor of a band of wagon travelers killed and cannibalized by their guide, one Colonel Ives. But "Colqhoun" is Ives and, seizing control of the camp, plots to turn it into a cannibal colony. He recognizes Boyd as a seeming kindred spirit, and the movie becomes a test of whether Boyd will succumb to Ives' pressure and his own Wendigo hunger.

"Ravenous" was a box office bomb in its day, grossing $2 million against a $12 million budget, and it received largely underwhelmed or confounded reviews. But don't take that as a mark against the movie, which has a following to this day. (Any "Yellowjackets" fan should make watching "Ravenous" a priority.)

For "Ravenous" to work, Boyd's temptation needs to feel real. When you've got someone as charismatic as Robert Carlyle playing Ives, it sure does. That performance isn't the only way that Carlyle saved the movie.

"Ravenous" had a tumultuous production, and Guy Pearce has called "Ravenous" his worst experience shooting a movie. The film's original director Milcho Manchevski was fired mid-filming with 20th Century Fox moving to replace him with "Home Alone 3" director Raja Gosnell. The cast rejected that, and so Carlyle brought in director Antonia Bird, who he'd worked with on the 1997 crime film "Face." Bird is the credited director of "Ravenous," but was she able to wrangle the mess she'd inherited?

Even a "Ravenous" fan will admit the movie is, tonally, all over the place. After a scene of Ives revealing his true murderous self, the movie breaks out into a chase scene with comical banjo music. If you'll pardon the pun, "Ravenous" bites off a lot and tests how much it's capable of chewing. But that strangeness is a strength, as there's no other movie quite like "Ravenous."

In a 2015 retrospective review for Rolling Stone, critic David Ehrlich showed the kind of praise that has earned "Ravenous" a fanbase. Ehrlich complimented its unique tonal recipe and how, through its setting, it equates manifest destiny colonialism with literal cannibalism... while conceding those qualities are likely what turned off audiences in 1999.

Considering the 1990s saw Anthony Hopkins make Hannibal Lecter into a cinematic icon on the heels "The Silence of the Lambs," I can see why studio execs would invest in cannibal horror. But "Ravenous" was just too weird a movie to ever be a massive hit, even though it's found its supporters with time.

#3399. ‘Aquamarine’ Reboot Series Officially Set With Original Cast Returning

After twenty years, the teen mermaid comedy Aquamarine is resurfacing. The 2006 film is getting a sequel series on Hulu, set two decades after the original. Plus, two cast members from the movie are back in action.

Directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum (Sneakerella), from a script by John Quaintance (Will and Grace) and Jessica Bendinger (Stick It) and loosely adapted from the 2001 novel of the same name by Alice Hoffman (Practical Magic), Aquamarine centers around two teenage friends, Claire (Emma Roberts, American Horror Story) and Hailey (Joanna "JoJo" Levesque, R.V.). The longtime Floridian friends are about to be separated when Hailey's family moves to Australia, but fate intervenes when a storm deposits a mermaid, the titular Aquamarine (Sara Paxton, Darcy's Wild Life), in a local swimming pool. She has three days to prove that true love exists before she's married off to a merman, so her new friends try to set her up with hunky local lifeguard Raymond (Jake McDornan, American Sniper). The movie was a moderate commercial success in theaters, but has become a cult hit on home video and streaming.

Thus, it's now returning as a TV series on Hulu and Disney+. Teenager Coral (Kenzi Richardson, Vampirina: Teenage Vampire) moves to a small town in Florida, where she begins to unravel the truth behind her mother's disappearance...only to learn that her mother was a mermaid, and that she's inherited strange aquatic superpowers. The series will also star Briella Guiza (Atlas), Theodore Dalton (A Wonderful Way With Dragons) and Annika Reese (Quads and the Kicker), plus Roberts and McDornan, who will reprise their roles from the original film. The series has been greenlit and is in development, but no release date has yet been announced.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Rosenbaum, who directed the original film, and Susan Cartsonis, who produced it, will executive produce the series alongside Melissa Carter (The Cleaning Lady), Roberts, and McDornan. Rosenbaum will direct the series' pilot, which will be written by Sarah Watson (The Bold Type).

Aquamarine is in development; no release date has yet been announced. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#3398. GTA 6's Staggering Sales Still Might Never Catch GTA 5

The new game's day-one sales defy belief, but so does its big brother's long-term record

On Friday, Rockstar Games' parent company Take-Two Interactive announced sales figures for Grand Theft Auto 6 that are so dizzying, I'm still processing them. They have clearly shattered preorder records for video games and launch sales — in fact, total sales – for just about any form of entertainment.

Take-Two said that GTA 6 sold 32.5 million copies during its pre-release period, and that through the end of launch day on Nov. 19, it had racked up $3.79 billion in revenue.

Comparisons are fun to make, but apt ones don't really exist. On its day of launch, GTA 6 had made twice as much money as Taylor Swift's entire Eras tour, and more than any film has ever made across a full theatrical run. Alinea Analytics reckons that by the end of the weekend the numbers were up to 44.9 million copies sold and a round $4 billion in revenue. It took GTA 6 one day to eclipse the lifetime sales figures of The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.

Here's a more meaningful comparison: Grand Theft Auto 5 took three days to hit $1 billion in sales. GTA 6's launch is four times bigger than its predecessor's. It will definitely crush GTA 5's lifetime record, right? Well… not necessarily.

As amazing as GTA 6's sales are, it has a long, long way to go to catch up with its big brother. GTA 5 is the second-best selling game of all time behind Minecraft (or third-best, depending on how you account for sales of Tetris). It has sold a staggering 235 million copies to date, more than two and a half times as many as the next game in the all-time ranking, Rockstar's own Red Dead Redemption 2.

When it comes to long-tail, long-term sales, GTA 5 is in a different class entirely — a class of two, alongside Minecraft. It's not a given that GTA 6 will necessarily be able to join this class. A few things have to fall into place.

Rockstar has yet to confirm a PC version of the game, for starters, though one is expected in 2027. That will unlock a whole new audience for GTA 6, especially globally, and supercharge its sales again.

Rockstar has also yet to confirm that it will create a GTA 6 version of GTA Online. GTA 5's scrappy multiplayer mode became a live-service behemoth that has driven a huge proportion of those 235 million sales, and that financially sustained Rockstar through the extremely long and expensive developments of Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 6. Analysts also seem confident in predicting GTA 6's online mode will arrive in 2027, although I think a degree of skepticism is warranted on that part.

Rockstar hasn't said one word publicly about GTA 6 Online for good reason. Migrating online gaming audiences, who’ve invested massive amounts of time and money in their accounts, from one game to a sequel is notoriously difficult. It's why there was never a World of Warcraft 2, for example, and there are vanishingly few examples of it being done successfully (Destiny 2 being, perhaps, the exception that proves the rule).

This is not to say that Rockstar won't do it, but the studio will need to be extremely careful and consider its strategy. Will it lock the new online mode behind a full purchase of GTA 6, as it initially did with its predecessor? Sell it separately and/or bundle it in a GTA Plus subscription, as it now does for GTA Online? Or maybe even go free-to-play? These approaches all have their advantages and drawbacks when it comes to tempting GTA Online players to upgrade and maximizing the new online game's revenue, but only one of them is going to help GTA 6 sell as many copies as GTA 5.

There's a final but important asterisk to consider with respect to GTA 5's astonishing sales. It has been released across three console generations, and a lot of those purchases will be duplicates or even triplicates (which is especially true for GTA Online players).

In other words, the sales figures are likely flattering to the maximum size of the GTA audience; I don't think there are 235 million GTA players out there. It's going to be challenging for GTA 6 to meet that number unless it, too, spans three generations. I hope we won't be waiting until late in the PlayStation 7's life for GTA 7, but you never know with Rockstar.

One thing's for sure: Rockstar's only real competition is itself. GTA 6 has had the biggest launch imaginable. Can it also go the distance?

#3397. Star Trek Officially Returns To The Deep Space Nine Era Today

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

The Star Trek franchise has spent the better part of the past six decades exploring different corners of the galaxy, expanding with each release, but in today's newest release, the franchise is revisiting the Star Trek: Deep Space Nine era among others. Although the original series established the foundation for what would become a sci-fi phenomenon, the TV and film productions that have come after Star Trek: The Original Series have all been able to explore further reaches of the universe, creating an undeniably thorough franchise. Some eras have become important to building the legacy, while others have helped bridge the gaps in the larger story.

Regardless of how popular an era has been, Star Trek has been able to introduce some of the most recognizable characters in modern fiction throughout the franchise, changing the face of sci-fi in TV, film, and on the page. Star Trek's TV presence, specifically, has fundamentally changed what a sci-fi drama on the small screen could accomplish, and continues to push the boundaries. Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, specifically, was a strong era for the franchise. Beginning in 1993, the series abandoned the typical format viewers were used to and explored long-running conflicts using a familiar crew and a stationary space station.

Now, as Star Trek celebrates its 60th anniversary as a franchise, revisiting some of its strongest eras has never been easier than with Star Trek Timelines, a brand-new release that comes out today, Tuesday, November 24. The official visual history of the franchise, Star Trek Timelines brings each of the show's eras into focus for a deep exploration.

Today's release of Star Trek Timelines: A Visual Voyage Through Generations of History marks a whole new exploration of the franchise and celebrates its milestone 60th anniversary. One of the most important eras of the franchise's history began with the debut of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine in 1993. The series, which saw a major departure from the traditional way Star Trek stories were told, was able to reinvigorate the franchise for a whole new generation of viewers. With the series having gone against the established formula that worked for the Star Trek franchise, Deep Space Nine opened new doors.

The show's stationary setting allowed Deep Space Nine to develop its plots with more depth, reaching for larger thematic elements and baking them into each story with a different type of precision than other franchise series had allowed for. A highly regarded era of the franchise, the new book breaks down the era visually, expanding on how the show's rich style and different elements allowed for an entirely different experience than what Star Trek enthusiasts had experienced before. Challenging the franchise on nearly every front, Deep Space Nine is one of the most important pieces of the Star Trek journey, and is honored in Star Trek Timelines.

Star Trek Timelines: A Visual Voyage Through Generations of History is available for purchase through this link.

With Star Trek Timelines, written by Derek Tyler Attico, Michael Dismuke, Kelli Fitzpatrick, and Jim Johnson, readers will be able to explore the franchise from its early beginnings through its latest series, all with the expert knowledge that comes from its authors. Examining the timelines of each series thoroughly, the book looks at alternate timelines as well, including the Mirror universe, the Kelvin timeline, and the Year of Hell storyline from Star Trek: Voyager. With character-focused spreads that trace each major figure's development through the franchise and a ton of information that Star Trek fans will enjoy, the book is a wonderful resource.

While Star Trek Timelines isn't exclusively dedicated to an exploration of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, the comprehensive approach of the book gives its readers the opportunity to explore major parts of the series and works through some of its most unique pieces. With over 300 pages of exploration and a foreword from Star Trek legend Kate Mulgrew, who played Captain Kathryn Janeway in Star Trek: Voyager, Star Trek Timelines provides its dedicated readers a chance to dig further into the franchise, looking at the Star Trek journey from a whole new vantage point.

#3396. Chris Evans Reveals Whether Avengers: Doomsday Shows Doctor Doom's Face Under The Mask

Marvel Studios certainly made an impression, for good or ill, when it announced at San Diego Comic-Con 2024 that Robert Downey Jr. would be returning to the Marvel Cinematic Universe... but as Doctor Doom, not Iron Man. Marvel fans instantly assumed, with good reason, that Doom was being reimagined as having some connection to Iron Man (i.e. that Victor von Doom would be a Tony Stark variant turned evil).

But surprisingly, the marketing for "Avengers: Doomsday" has not been leaning on any connection between Doom and Iron Man. The second "Doomsday" trailer confirms that he comes from the Fantastic Four's universe, Earth-828, and shares a history with them. The closest thing has been a new post-credits scene from "Avengers Endgame: Encore" that shows Doom forging his mask in a way mirroring Tony doing so back in 2008's "Iron Man." Speaking to Empire, Marvel Studios President Kevin Feige also stressed that, despite the double casting, RDJ's Doom is indeed Victor von Doom and not a Tony Stark variant.

Now, there is an easy out here. Doom is famous for wearing a metal mask to hide his supposedly scarred face. In the comics, he almost never takes that mask off. If it wanted, Marvel Studios could keep Doom in the mask and make it so him sharing an actor with Tony Stark becomes a non-issue. In fact, Chris Evans told Empire that's exactly what happens in "Doomsday," explaining:

"[Doom is] wearing a mask the whole time. That's not an easy challenge, to try and get your message across and be emotionally available to connect with. It just reinforces what I've always felt: Downey can do anything."

It feels pretty implausible Marvel would hire RDJ like this and not take full advantage of him, but I want to believe it.

When "Doomsday" directors Joe and Anthony Russo announced Robert Downey Jr. as Doom on the SDCC stage, they said they felt they needed the "greatest actor in the world" to play the villain. Chris Evans' words to Empire echo that narrative: Downey is Doom only because he's the best actor for the part.

And in a vacuum, sure, yes, there's little doubt he can pull it off. During his MCU hiatus, RDJ won an Oscar for his turn in Christopher Nolan's "Oppenheimer" as Lewis Strauss, who destroys J. Robert Oppenheimer's (Cillian Murphy) life out of a petty, misplaced grudge. Strauss is to "Oppie" as Doom is to Reed Richards!

But when you bring back your franchise's biggest star in a different role? And as part of a story that's all about different versions of characters from different universes colliding? Yeah, you can't blame people for assuming there's going to be an in-universe reason for Stark and Doom sharing a face.

This is pure speculation, but one going theory in Marvel fan communities is that Downey's casting as Doom is a smokescreen to hide that he'll also be returning as Iron Man in "Avengers: Secret Wars" (i.e. there's no need to hide him on the "Secret Wars" set because everyone will already know he's there playing Doom). You could pull that off if Doom indeed wears his mask the entire time, so the films don't present him and Stark as twins, and that bypasses the issue of RDJ getting no facetime if Doom keeps his mask on. I'll admit this appeals to me because it keeps Doom and Stark separate, which has always been my preference. But again, no clue if that's even remotely true.

It's worth noting that Chris Evans is also only talking about "Avengers: Doomsday." Perhaps that film will have Doom keep his mask on the whole time, and then only in "Secret Wars" will Doom be unmasked. There's some narrative sense to that: Part one of this story builds up Doom's threat, and then once he's won, you can explore the man underneath. In the original 1984 "Secret Wars" comics, after Doom steals the power of the godlike Beyonder, he uses it to heal his scarred face.

An adaptation of that scene practically writes itself. Doom, revealing his new power, unlatches his mask and shows himself free of any scarring. But this time, some of the heroes recognize Doom's face as Tony Stark's, and that opens up a mystery of why they look identical.

For what it's worth, Doom's co-creator Jack Kirby always maintained Doom's face being "horribly scarred" was an exaggeration. No, Doom actually only has a small scar on his chin, but he's such an insecure egotist that he can't stand to let anyone — even himself — see that reminder of his imperfections, no matter how small they are. That's my preferred interpretation of comics Doom, but I'm not convinced crowded, multiverse-shattering blockbuster movies like "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars" will have room for that sort of psychological nuance.

"Avengers: Doomsday" is scheduled for theatrical release on December 18, 2026.

#3393. Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday Might Have The Biggest Box Office Opening Weekend Ever

There has been much discussion as to whether or not the Marvel Cinematic Universe has lost its lustre in recent years. Indeed, Marvel's 2025 box office proved the MCU has fallen from grace, at least in terms of launching newer or less surefire franchises. However, "The Avengers" remains a gold standard for audiences around the world, and "Avengers: Doomsday" is going to prove that in a big way In December. So much so that we could be looking at, quite literally, the biggest opening weekend of all time.

Directed by Joe and Anthony Russo, aka the Russo Brothers, "Doomsday" is currently expected to open with a whopping $375 to $424 million domestically on the weekend of December 18, per Box Office Theory. Mind you, that's just in North America, not worldwide. If this pans out, even on the low end, it would set a new high bar for cinema, financially speaking. "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" ruled the box office back in July with a record $360 million domestic debut, yet "Doomsday" looks like it might clear that with ease.

Even more surprising? The latest "Avengers" film is opening directly against the much-anticipated "Dune: Part Three," which is eyeing a blockbuster debut in the $91 to $115 million range. As a result, the so-called cinematic double bill known as Dunesday will blow Barbenheimer out of the water at the box office.

The latest "Avengers" cinematic event follows beloved heroes from three distinct universes as they're set on a deadly collision course and face an existential threat unlike anything they've ever encountered. Namely, Doctor Doom, played by former "Iron Man" star Robert Downey Jr. The Russos previously helmed both "Avengers: Infinity War" and "Avengers: Endgame," which also bodes well.

"Avengers: Doomsday" trailers are selling the film as the MCU's biggest event yet, and, much like "Infinity War" did in 2018, it's teeing up something even bigger. Specifically, "Avengers: Secret Wars," which will close out the MCU's Multiverse Saga by adapting one of the most beloved Marvel Comics storylines of all time.

It can't be emphasized just how staggering these numbers are. "Avengers: Endgame" smashed box office records with a $1.2 billion global opening in 2019, with its $357.1 million domestic figure serving as the opening weekend record until "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" came along. "Avengers: Endgame" also passed "Avatar" to reclaim the highest-grossing movie title earlier this year thanks to the "Encore" re-release. Its lifetime total sits at $2.94 billion worldwide.

In light of how up and down things have been for the MCU in recent years, there was doubt as to whether or not "Doomsday" could live up to sky high expectations. Evidently, audiences are still very interested in seeing Earth's Mightiest Heroes, despite anything else that's happened in the 2020s. It doesn't matter that "The Marvels" finished its box office run as the lowest-grossing MCU movie ever or that films like "Thunderbolts*" fell way short of commercial expectations. This is the Avengers.

Even more amazing is the fact that Disney and Marvel Studios are doing this without the benefit of IMAX screens. "Dune: Part Three" has those locked up, which is significant since IMAX has proved it's more important to the box office than ever before. But the Avengers don't need IMAX. Would it be nice? Sure, but they're going to shatter records either way.

"Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3392. ‘Parks and Rec’ Showrunner Teases a Very Different Turn for Amy Poehler’s New Peacock Series

When Amy Poehler and Mike Schur get together, sitcom magic happens. We saw it with Parks and Recreation, as Poehler's Leslie Knope inspired and entertained us for seven seasons. And over a decade later, that magic is still alive with their newest series, Dig. Adapted from Kate Myers' book Excavations, Poehler stars as Elise DeBellnick, a career archaeologist who runs the annual summer dig in Greece for Dr. Neville Wycombe (Hugh Laurie). While he's charming and pompous, she’s hardworking, straightforward, and has never had her own excavation. When she uncovers an artifact from an overlooked pit, she decides to make her own mark on herstory. The series also stars Geraldine Viswanathan, Max Greenfield, and Kayvan Novak.

Ahead of DIG's release, Collider sat down with Mike Schur and J.J. Philbin to discuss their new Peacock series. The showrunners unpack their collaboration with Poehler and why they were drawn to the Kate Myers novel. Plus, Schur teases what A Man on the Inside fans can expect in its final season. You can watch the full interview in the video above, or you can read the transcript below.

COLLIDER: You both have been behind some excellent series in the past. Talk to me about why DIG was the next story that you wanted to do.

MIKE SCHUR: Because Amy Poehler called me on the phone and said she wanted to adapt the book into a show. That's why. She's the one who found it. She read it. She really locked into the main character of the book. She's been doing so much producing, directing, and developing for the last 12 years since Parks ended. She just really found it. She knew it. She saw it. She knew what it was. Then asked me if I wanted to develop it with her, and the answer was a very quick "yes."

When I read it, and I think when J.J. read it too, we both saw immediately what she had seen, which was an interesting setting, great character for her to play, very different from other characters she's played in her life. But also, putting her in a workplace comedy with women of different ages that we started to think of all four women as the same woman just at four different points in their life. What you would do if you were surrounded by previous versions of yourself, and the ways that you would love them and feel for them, but also the ways that those versions of you would drive you crazy, and you'd be embarrassed by them. And then the central metaphor of digging: digging through the past to get to the truth is a great central metaphor. If Amy had called and said, "I'd like to adapt the 'Los Angeles Yellow Pages,'" I would've been like, "Great, let's get to it." But in this case, she found a book that really had a lot of juicy stuff in it that made a good show.

J.J. PHILBIN: Mike had told me early on, I think you guys had breakfast. He said, "I had breakfast with Amy, and she pitched me this idea," and I was like, "Oh my gosh, I'm so excited." Just for myself as a viewer to be able to watch it on TV and hear about it as you guys make this TV show. Like every woman who works in comedy, it's just a dream to work with Amy Poehler. When Mike suggested that I come on board, I was just thrilled, really delighted. We'd never worked together before, so that was also just an interesting experiment. We've been married for 21 years. Let's see what that's like.

SCHUR: Well, we immediately got divorced. [Laughs]

PHILBIN: We moved to separate parts of the house. [Laughs] You know, it's funny, I don't know if this was right or not, but we didn't go into it with a lot of ground rules. We sort of said, "Let's see what it feels like," and it was immediately so easy and fun that I'm glad that we didn't torture it by going in saying, like, "You're going to pitch this. No, I'm going to pitch that."

SCHUR: As soon as Amy and I realized that J.J. was the right person to do this with us, my immediate thought was, "Is that going to be weird?" And then my second immediate thought was, "It's going to be fine." We never sat down and had a big discussion about who was going to do what. I had this gut instinct that after both working in TV comedy for 25 or 30 years, it was going to be fine. And then it was fine. It was super fun. We had a great time. We had a very easy time with it. The labor divided up very effortlessly. We were like, "Why don't you do this, and I'll do this." It was about as easy and fun as I think it could have possibly been.

PHILBIN: It's really convenient to live with your co-showrunner so that you can go home from work and keep talking about things as you do the dishes and walk the dog. So a lot of the show got broken while we were driving our kids to places. So that part made it feel very effortless and nice.

That's such a great way to take it. I know some people like to separate work from their home life. But to bring it in and figure this out together, that's so cool.

SCHUR: Yeah, it was really fun. Again, we just did it separately. So our time at home was usually spent with her telling me what problems they were encountering whatever show she was on, and me doing the same for my shows. We just kept doing that except it was the same show. That's the only difference.

You brought up Amy, and you've worked with her for many years. How has your relationship with Amy evolved over time, and what was it like working with her specifically on this?

SCHUR: The only difference between this and Parks and Rec is that, technically speaking, she didn't create the show with me. I created it with Greg Daniels, and then she was the other collaborator. By the time that show ended, it felt like a thing that she and I had been doing together. It really felt like I was in charge of half of it, and she was in charge of half of it. Our decisions were creatively made together. We had a rule on that show, with the whole cast really, with her as the captain, that when something would come up, it's like, if everyone wants to do this, we do it. And if one person vetoes it, then we say no.

That's always been the way. It's very democratic. So the only difference with this is that we were in it from the very beginning. And I'm not kidding, it felt like when we started talking about this show, it felt like yesterday Parks and Rec ended, and then today we started something new. It felt like we picked up right where we left off, and it's been a dream.

PHILBIN: I would say it's really fun to watch Amy and Mike work together. They have such a respectful and easy collaboration, and they really make each other laugh. I think that kind of spreads throughout the set and into the writers' room, and everybody just gets that teamwork is the way that we make this show. It's so nice to have that dynamic at the top of the call sheet, just defining for everybody what the vibe is going to be on set and in the room.

You are both booked and busy. You both have two mystery shows that you have about to come out. What can you preview about the new season of Only Murders in the Building and A Man on the Inside?

PHILBIN: I was not a part of Season 6. The last season that I worked on Only Murders was Season 5, and then I went straight from that show to DIG. I'm excited to watch Only Murders...

SCHUR: A Man on the Inside was really fun to make this year. We shot almost the entire thing in San Francisco. It's a celebration of that city, which is a city I truly love, and it's very much an homage to other movies and TV shows that were shot in San Francisco, so there are a lot of fun Easter eggs and stuff that people will enjoy if they're familiar with those other movies.
