#3391. Cliff Booth Stars Explain How David Fincher & Quentin Tarantino Shaped Their Performances

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the first time in nearly a decade that audiences can see acclaimed filmmaker Quentin Tarantino's work in theaters. While the sequel to 2019's love letter to American cinema, Once Upon a Time in... Hollywood, was directed by David Fincher, Tarantino still penned the screenplay. The combination of both powerhouses has made the movie one of the year's most anticipated, and the cast even felt the magic while working on set.

Brad Pitt once again plays Cliff Booth, who now finds himself in 1977 without the trusty Rick Dalton by his side. While he is no longer at the center of Hollywood, he still hangs out with famous folk within the industry, doing their dirty work in the seedy underbelly of Los Angeles. He runs into various fascinating characters, including actor Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), whose tension with his wife Toni (Carla Gugino) becomes central to the plot. Charlie's agent, Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), finds herself entangled with Cliff romantically, while Blaxploitation movie star Roderick "Hot Rod" Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) adds plenty of charm to the proceedings.

ScreenRant's Kim Horcher interviewed Caan, Debicki, Gugino, and Abdul-Mateen about the exciting challenge of stepping into Tarantino's world through the lens of Fincher's camera in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. The actors shared their reactions to joining the project, how they got into character, and which they found to be the best parts of fictional 1970s Hollywood.

ScreenRant: How was it working with Fincher on a Tarantino project? How did it feel to get that call?

Carla Gugino: It's pretty much the best call you could ever get, honestly. I think it's almost as simple as that. You have the foundation of this incredible script, and then you have one of the greatest visionary directors interpreting it through his lens. And that combination is so unique. I don't know that we'll ever get that kind of combination. It's such an unusual opportunity. It's like falling into a pot of honey.

Yahya Abdul-Mateen II: It makes the job easy. We both have a theater background. When I go to do theater, I get a chance to say the best words, and that helps a lot. We had everything that we needed in order to succeed, and so the stage was set for us to just bring the best of ourselves without having to figure out how to make things work so much, which sometimes is what we have to do.

The job is to figure out how to make things work. But sometimes when you have to do that less, then you can just get in there, and it's just about what you get to do. "Ooh, I get to do this." That's what work felt like on most days for me. I felt like a star.

This project was a gift, a throwback to a really, really fun time. And to make a present-day movie that is a '70s movie with the flair of Quentin Tarantino's words, and under the direction of David Fincher's eye with Brad and the entire cast? It was just really, really fun.

Carla Gugino: I think the thing about Quentin's writing that's so noticeable is that nothing is ever generic. You really believe these people are real people. It's a lot like Elmore Leonard, where they act in unexpected ways. When most people are nervous, they're flirty. He brings the period to life in a really exceptional way.

And then David is so known for how impeccable he is with period stuff, so I [love] the fact that we got to embody this world of the '70s and what it represents. There's this star, and we have a stunt guy who is kind of in awe of that star. We have a lifelong actress who's made a living that way, but hasn't been as successful as she wants to be, but also is kind of okay with that. Then we have a TV star who gets a taste of all the different elements of Hollywood at that time. Everybody is sort of compromised, and that's kind of what the '70s was like in a lot of ways. So, all those things are very noticeable.

ScreenRant: Elizabeth, your character really surprised me with her somewhat contradictory nature and her multidimensionality. I feel like I've met people like her in LA. What was she to you?

Elizabeth Debicki: She was an amazing role that I found in that script. I think Quentin created a character that is quite unlike anything else he's written for a female character. She is really contradictory, and I think that is the core of human nature. We just roam around and contradict ourselves.

She obviously has real agency in this world, but she's really smart and funny and completely not ready for someone to walk into her life to kind of force her to look at herself. It's a really interesting relationship between her and Cliff, and I loved playing her.

When David and I first spoke about it, I remember us both saying our goal really was that we really wanted her to feel real, like someone you knew. I wanted her to feel like, "I know that woman. I wonder what she ate for breakfast. I bet she lives in an apartment that looks like that." She feels grounded.

ScreenRant: Scott, on the other hand, I feel like I've only met maybe one or two Charlies. What went into making him your own?

Scott Caan: Listen, Quentin writes really great characters, and when I read the script, I was like, "Wow, this one is fantastic." For me, I like to bring as much of myself into the character as I can. For this one, initially, it was like, "God, how do I justify all this stuff?" That was really my approach. "How can I justify all my behavior and all these decisions?" And it was very fun.

There's one [actor he reminded me of], which I'm not even going to mention who it is, but there was one idea. We were talking about it before, but it kind of went away. We do a lot of homework, and then when you show up, you kind of forget it all and just go try to play. I mean, the guy's got to be a version of me. So, I read something, and I go, "Alright, how can I put the version of me into this?"

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth begins playing in select IMAX theaters on November 25 before streaming December 23 on Netflix.

#3389. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

File size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

#3388. You Can Get One of These Pocket E-Readers for As Little As $55 Before Black Friday

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3387. Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series

The other day, one line in an otherwise unremarkable marketing email caught my eye: “Discovery is exactly what fans come to Netflix for.”

Even with a dangling preposition (in a press release littered with errors), the claim felt like the more glaring mistake: Netflix is where fans go for discovery. They do? Still? Are you sure about that?

But when it comes to Netflix’s core business — streaming television — the service is largely a preferred destination by default. Being an industry pioneer helped establish Netflix as a utility among TV fans, many of whom still turn to it when they want to see “what’s on,” but it’s hard to imagine why anyone would head there first when searching for their next favorite show.

That would require the customer to trust Netflix — either as the service offering the most bang for their buck, the shows everyone is talking about, or, most likely and simplest of all, the best series on TV. Can the streamer really stake a claim to any of those distinctions?

Throughout 2026, Netflix has been plagued by problems and complaints. Viewership for returning seasons is dwindling, subscription prices are rising, hot new franchises are scarce, and high-quality programming — a subjective designation, to be sure — isn’t what it used to be. Netflix is no longer the most affordable SVOD service. It’s not the most award-winning, nor is it the buzziest.

A sustainable hit could quiet things down, but those have been hard to come by. Netflix’s most popular new shows this year were limited series (like “His & Hers” and “I Will Find You”), which only offer short-term juice. Promising first seasons (“The Boroughs”) faced quick cancellations that left fans fuming and analysts searching for answers. Even touted chart toppers (“Man on Fire”) don’t get a quick Season 2 renewal, let alone a quick turnaround between seasons.

Ignoring these very-online narratives, none of the aforementioned shows earned rave reviews, and the streamer’s awards output echoed what’s felt like a dearth in quality. Total Emmy wins were cut nearly in half this year, from 30 to 16, causing Netflix to fall to third place (behind HBO and Apple) for the first time since topping the town in 2021.

A month after Emmy night, all the criticism reached a crescendo when a plunging stock price and lack of hits forced mass layoffs, including the dismissal of chief content officer Bela Bajaria and other key executives. Peter Rice is at the helm now, and his new team is setting the table for changes in 2027 — much like Netflix did in 2022 after The Great Streaming Correction opened the door for an ad-tier and shut the door on password sharing.

While it would be foolish to believe fixing one aspect of a diverse business would make all its other problems go away, it would be equally foolish to pretend there’s not a TV problem at Netflix. A healthy TV slate only benefits engagement across the platform, and the streamer is still the big dog in SVOD — it’s just losing ground year by year. So what’s to be done?

Well, that depends on how much Netflix is willing to change. If it’s all on the table, there are a handful of reasonable shifts they could make to improve their reputation. If not, well, I’ve got an idea for that, too.

At the root of Netflix’s TV problem is that its shows feel disposable. Sometimes that’s by design: Netflix makes a lot of programs that can be watched while scrolling, which can be OK. TV has long been a medium built for background entertainment, and it’s still nice to have an easily digestible distraction while doing dishes or folding laundry.

But Netflix may have gone too far. Setting aside quality (for a moment), the streamer’s focus on “discovery” paired with its faith in the almighty algorithm to sort through its substantial monthly programming influx emphasizes new shows above all else. There’s always another new series, new special, or new live event to watch, but there isn’t always more of the show you already love. Some original series take years between releasing new seasons. Some only dole out six or eight episodes every 18 months. Some get canceled after one or two seasons, and very few run more than three or four seasons in total.

Whether or not the approach works from a financial perspective, it fails to foster audience investment, and investment is where TV thrives. Just look at this year’s most-watched shows on streaming, per Nielsen: “Stranger Things” holds down the No. 1 spot, but then it’s “Bluey,” “The Pitt,” “Grey’s Anatomy,” and “The Big Bang Theory.” Keep scrolling and it’s even easier to spot the dominant trend: Shows with huge libraries that first aired on network TV.

These are the kind of shows that people keep up with for years, decades, or more. They like the characters, they like the structure, they like the setting — they like being in the show’s world, whether it’s a hospital filled with hot doctors or a nerd’s living room. Offering access on a regular basis encourages investment, which breeds loyalty, which creates longevity. Producing more episodes, more often — like broadcast TV has done all along — creates bigger libraries that fans will happily live in for years on end because they enjoy spending time with those characters and within those stories.

Streamers have been reluctant to adopt their predecessor’s production model (for reasons both valid and ridiculous that I’ll get into in the next section), but the success of long-running (and long-gone) broadcast series on streaming, paired with the recent popularity of “The Pitt,” makes it hard to argue against making longer seasons, consisting of more episodes, that are released on a regular basis. It’s what audiences want now, and it’s what they’ve shown they’ll want later.

Which brings us to the binge model. One of the reasons Netflix hasn’t experimented with more broadcast-style streaming shows (like “The Pitt”) is because it can’t. Its release model is different. The binge model requires everything be done before anything premieres, including timely post-production work like subtitles and dubbing, which Netflix needs to serve its global base. While episodes of most network series are still being written, shot, and edited as earlier, completed episodes roll out, episodes of a Netflix series drop all at once.

Luckily, Netflix already made the change. Or started to, at least.

Nowadays, Netflix’s most popular original series are often released in batches (or “parts”), including the last two seasons of “Stranger Things” and “Bridgerton.” Both shows are among the most-watched programs on the planet, so the shift in release strategy hasn’t hurt their popularity. Other shows are already released weekly, like “The Great British Baking Show,” or close to weekly, like “Love Is Blind.”

Moreover, the addition of live events has forced Netflix to implement new tactics to raise awareness for time-sensitive content (instead of just relying on the algorithm), which should limit fears over viewer confusion. (For seasons released in parts, the Netflix platform tends to list how many episodes will be released and when. You can even set reminders for upcoming programming, even if none of it is available yet — like, say, the NFL game on Thanksgiving Eve, which is a thing, I guess.)

Netflix decided long ago to break up the binge, now they just need to keep going. After all, the binge model was created to disrupt Hollywood. No one was releasing full seasons at once, and Netflix executives recognized how DVDs had primed viewers to marathon TV shows. Instead of old favorites (like “The Office”), why not give them new ones to devour?

But Netflix isn’t a disruptor anymore. It’s the industry leader. It doesn’t need a gimmick to draw attention. It needs a strategy to help keep it.

A weekly release model could help. Netflix doesn’t need to enforce it on every series — let people binge “Ginny & Georgia” — but for shows that could benefit from the regular cycle of anticipation, fulfillment, dissection (repeat), the tried-and-true strategy could do wonders for audience investment. In the short-term, it could help prevent dips in engagement and help foster engagement with newly beloved series. In the long-term, it could help build franchises, libraries, and loyalty.

You can’t just make the next “Pitt.” You have to create the system to support it.

Speaking of support, it’s time to talk about quality. What constitutes a good show and a bad show will always, in the end, remain in the eye of the beholder, but a company aiming to “replace all television” can’t rely on subjective interpretations to define its brand. Nor can it rely primarily on an algorithm to elevate the best options instead of the easiest ones. Otherwise, you risk a narrative like this year’s, where objective measurements like ratings (where the three most-watched new shows average a 56 rating on Metacritic) and awards (where Netflix landed one more win than NBC and Peacock combined) create the impression of less-than-“gourmet” service.

Some such schemes are already underway with pre-show ads running before episodes and prominent brand campaigns helping connect viewers with their new favorite programs. Hopefully, that signals more old-school advocacy efforts are coming. Eventize episodes, not just new seasons. Build channels for episodic programs to elevate their best moments. Add permanent subsections to Netflix’s genre listings.

This is not a new idea. At various times for various reasons, various experts have suggested Netflix launch a free subscription tier in order to promote its growing library to a wider audience. FAST (free, ad-supported streaming) platforms like Pluto, Tubi, and The Roku Channel are growing quickly mainly by replicating the broadcast model for the streaming age, and Netflix could take a page out of their playbook to expand their business in any number of ways. But in terms of solving their TV problem, they should use it to distinguish their premium original programming from their recent obsession: YouTube slop.

I’ll be honest: I don’t think of Netflix and YouTube as competitors, mainly because Netflix isn’t free. Sure, there’s YouTube Premium, but YouTube is instantly accessible, sans subscription, and that’s how most users get hooked. I don’t care how many more hours people spend watching YouTube than Netflix because the hours I spend watching movie trailers, how-to-videos, and late-night clips are not the same as the hours I spend watching “Little House on the Prairie,” “Long Story Short,” and “East of Eden.” One I’m willing to pay for, one I’m not. So the idea that Netflix, as a business, should be trying to surpass YouTube never made sense to me.

It still doesn’t, but I understand the market demands constant growth, and I understand why Netflix would want YouTube’s viewers, especially in the younger demographic. So Netflix has been busy signing content creators, adding podcasts, and filling the service with easy-listening videos (aka videos you don’t need to watch, but can play in the background without much disturbance). If that helps bring the next generation to Netflix so they can discover the glory of “BoJack Horseman,” great! But right now, BoJack is sitting side by side with random content like “Conspiracy Theories,” “Small Town Murder,” and “Bill Simmons.”

That’s a problem. We shouldn’t equate those very distinct experiences, and Netflix shouldn’t suggest we do. At best, it builds a false equivalency that steadily lowers our artistic standards for visual entertainment. At worst, it leads to more fans of this “Bill Simmons.”

So let’s create some tiers. Launch a free version of Netflix where all the podcasts, creator videos, and short-form content can live. Make money the old-fashioned way — from ads — while offering select TV shows to sample in the hopes viewers will get hooked and pay for an upgraded subscription. Keep original series, movies, and other top library offerings on the paid tiers, and structure those however you like. (Currently, there’s Standard with Ads, Standard, and Premium, each with their distinct perks.)

Is creating a FAST version of Netflix a whole lot of work to dispel the notion that Netflix makes too much disposable TV? Yup, and I won’t pretend to know how feasible it is, financially or otherwise. But Netflix needs to take a big swing or two if it hopes to fix its reputation, which brings us to my last option.

Netflix is still the dominant streamer in Hollywood. Plentiful stats support its case, but why look any further than how many other streamers license content to their biggest competitor? Disney+, Hulu, Paramount+, and more each lend their once-exclusive series to their rival in the hope of getting the Netflix bump (or a quick influx of cash). Never did I think I’d see the day where HBO would be available on another streamer, and yet everything from “Sex and the City” to “Ballers” has graced Netflix in 2026.

With that in mind, Netflix may choose to stay the course. The once-and-future tech company is notorious for sticking to certain brand tenets, like trusting the algorithm over traditional marketing and its binge model over traditional release strategies. Even when Hollywood pushes back, Netflix’s broader goals continue to evolve. Originally, it wanted to be the HBO of streaming. Then it wanted to replace cable. Then it wanted to replace all television.

What it wants to be now isn’t so clear. Wall Street keeps forcing comparisons to YouTube, some of which are invited by Netflix’s pursuit of its content and podcast creators. Maybe Netflix executives believe they can raise their market cap with vertical videos and video game previews, with new decision-makers and added theatrical grosses, with a few small tweaks here and a few surprise wins there. It has the leverage to wait out complaints and keep making TV exactly as it has been, if it so chooses.

But because of its relative health, I hope Netflix sees its TV problem as more of a TV opportunity. Yes, it needs more hits. Yes, it needs to build back trust. But it also wants to grow, and the suggestions above are all about sustainable growth through better TV. Longer seasons, more episodes, weekly releases, stronger support, clearer delineations, a FAST service — none of these ideas are revolutionary. They’re not meant to be. They’re meant to give the people what they want.

If Netflix is going to be where fans go for discovery, it first needs to be a place they can trust to get what what they need.

#3386. How to get your car out of the impound in GTA 6

There's the easy way and the expensive way

There's the easy way and the expensive way

It doesn't take long for one of your cars to end up at the police impound in Grand Theft Auto 6. You might have abandoned it near a crime scene, or they arrested you while you were driving it. While the circumstances may vary, you have only two ways to proceed if a car is impounded: you forget about it or you retrieve it.

If you are not ready to abandon your favorite car and want it back, we've got you covered. Here's how to get your car out of the impound in GTA 6.

There are two methods to retrieve a car from the police impound: you can either steal it back or pay for it. Both are valid, but the second one becomes available only in Chapter 2.

Stealing the car is the most plausible and cheapest option to execute. You just need to head to the impound lot, enter, and drive your car away from there. Some impounds, like the one in Port Gellhorn, have openings that you can use to enter unnoticed. Regardless of how you get inside, the challenge is escaping from the police once you leave. You must be prepared to run away, so try to come up with an escape route by setting a destination far from the city.

Now, the second option requires the Scooter Bros app, which you unlock in Chapter 2 after completing Moses' mission. If you have it already, open the app and select the impounded car (the one with a police badge icon). You will see that the first option in the menu is to pay a fee to retrieve the car.

The price varies depending on how far you are from the police impound. For example, I would have to pay $699 to get my car back from the Port Gellhorn impound while in Vice City. However, if you have upgraded your Scooter Bros account to Premium, you can use your remaining daily credits to request an impounded vehicle. Since this will essentially consume all your credits for the day, you should wait until you have only one left before using this option.

#3384. CBS Officially Confirms Major Schedule Change for ‘FBI’ and ‘CIA’

While not as long-running on CBS as NCIS or as storied as other Dick Wolf franchises, FBI is nearing a decade of patrolling the streets of the Big Apple and has built a following all its own. In that time, the elite agents of the New York field office have teamed up with other spin-offs, changed nights, and generally experienced a lot of shuffling as the Eye sets its schedule each season. This fall, both the flagship and its spin-off, CIA, saw another change, moving up an hour with no comedy block to account for, while Harlan Coben's Final Twist Season 2 took up the later 10 p.m. slot. Those used to the old lineup won't have to wait long for things to shift back, though.

CBS set midseason premiere dates for its entire primetime slate last week, beginning on Wednesday, January 6. For FBI fans, however, the date to watch is Monday, January 25, when the original series and CIA return to continue their ninth and second seasons, respectively. The procedurals will move back into a schedule more akin to last winter, taking up the 9 p.m. and 10 p.m. time slots once more to make room for a new hour of comedy. For the first time, Ghosts will be haunting two nights a week, taking up the 8 p.m. spot on Monday, in addition to its typical Thursday slot, during Season 6, while Joe Port and Joe Wiseman's new supernatural sitcom, Eternally Yours, takes up residence at 8:30 p.m. on Mondays.

The FBI franchise shuffling is on the lighter end of CBS' changes to the schedule this winter. Starting Sunday, January 17, Cupertino, the new legal thriller from The Good Wife creators Robert and Michelle King, will air at the very end of the weekend in the 10 p.m. time slot, making way for Matlock to return for Season 3 at 10 p.m. on Thursdays alongside Elsbeth. The all-NCIS block is also getting a shake-up, with Origins returning for two episodes to close out its shortened third season before NCIS: Sydney returns for its ten-episode Season 4 run on January 26. One new scripted series is also penciled in to premiere during the midseason — Einstein. Starring Criminal Minds alum Matthew Gray Gubler, the new mystery series will slot in on Sunday at 8 p.m. starting on February 12 following the Season 5 finale of Fire Country.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Three episodes of FBI Season 9 and CIA Season 2 remain before the holidays begin, and CBS' lineup takes off until midseason. Neither series will be taking it easy heading into the break, though. For the flagship, next week's episode, "22 minutes," will see the New York agents racing to stop a drug lord who murdered a DEA informant and now plans to take out the 16-year-old girl who saw everything. While that unfolds, Isobel (Alana de la Garza) pressures Maggie (Missy Peregrym) to rein in her relationship with OA (Zeeko Zaki) after his return from going undercover with Anna Vorpe left him in a troubled state. CIA, meanwhile, will air "Burned Rubber," following Colin (Tom Ellis) and Bill (Nick Gehlfuss) on a mission to save Colin's asset from an international crime group by uncovering a high-profile car theft ring that could lead to his whereabouts.

After next week, the two branches will once again link up in the CIA episode "Past Lives" on December 7. Nikki (Necar Zadegan) calls in some backup in the form of Jubal Valentine (Jeremy Sisto) after one of her former assets and their family suddenly vanish from their suburban block. However, as the team investigates further, the question becomes whether their allegiances have flipped or if their lives are all in danger. It'll be a welcome return for Jubal, who first introduced strait-laced FBI agent Bill Goodman to the joint operation and the more complicated world of spycraft in the series premiere.

FBI Season 9 and CIA Season 2 will make their midseason premieres on CBS on January 25 at 9 p.m. ET/PT and 10 p.m. ET/PT. Stay tuned here at Collider for further updates on both series as their winter break nears.

#3383. The Mosquito Bowl Won’t Let You Forget What It’s Really About

In this ScreenRant Cover Story, director Peter Berg and original author Buzz Bissinger break down the harrowing new war movie coming to Netflix.

On Christmas Eve in 1944, on the Pacific island of Guadalcanal, two regiments of US Marines training for the invasion of Okinawa played a game of football. That game is, ostensibly, the subject of The Mosquito Bowl, the new film from director Peter Berg that will be available to stream on Netflix from November 25, as well as the 2022 nonfiction book by Buzz Bissinger that inspired it. Considering the pairing of Berg and Bissinger once yielded Friday Night Lights, you might feel like you've heard enough to know what you're in for.

I can assure you, you have not. The Mosquito Bowl is in some ways about football – it is certainly about a handful of football players – but it's really a movie about war, and everything war costs. It follows four young men with hopes, dreams, and plenty of talent on the gridiron, who are diverted from whatever paths their lives may have taken and sent into a world of horrific violence and death. A world that is quite shockingly depicted.

"The goal of the movie was to grab the audience by the throat and make them feel something," Berg told ScreenRant's Liam Crowley in an interview alongside Bissinger. "To make something that feels like a participatory experience, not a spectator experience. I've had people see this film, and after it's like, 'Jesus Christ, I need to just go be quiet.'"

For this ScreenRant Cover Story, Berg and Bissinger talked us through what went into The Mosquito Bowl to create such a gripping watch, from its relationship to the true story and the real people that lived it to the quartet of actors and practical filmmaking that brought their experience to life.

Peter Berg and Buzz Bissinger have been looking for more opportunities to collaborate since Friday Night Lights. Creatively, they just clicked. "I don't think Buzz is the only genius writer out there," Berg told us, "but he is a genius writer, and he's my kind of genius writer."

"We knew each other, we knew each other's movements," Bissinger said. Plus, "we are actually legitimate second cousins."

Each time Bissinger embarked on a new writing project, he'd talk to Berg to see if it had big screen potential. But when he started work on what would become The Mosquito Bowl: A Game of Life and Death in World War II, he knew he had something that his cousin would be interested in.

BISSINGER: [In] 2018-2019, when I was beginning to write it, I told him about it. "Pete, this is perfect for you. It involves war, it involves football. You can blow a lot of things up. I think it's great."

Berg, for his part, got the same feeling, even before he had a chance to read the finished book.

BERG: I just could tell he was kind of on one. He was feeling it, he was doing intense research. I was getting the same energy from him that I got when I started reading Friday Night Lights and hearing that he had moved his family to Odessa, Texas, for a year and was living with this football team. I just sensed that. And knowing him as I do, and having read so many of his articles for Vanity Fair when he was just writing these incredible exposés on different aspects of American culture – I find him to be uniquely American in his perspective. I just knew that there was going to be something in the heart and the soul of what he was doing that was going to be very emotional for me and that I'd be able to connect to.

Bissinger's research came with some serious challenges. For one, of the 65 men who participated in the real Mosquito Bowl, "64 were dead by the time I got involved." Speaking to the last surviving player didn't prove all that helpful: "He honestly said, 'I don't remember what I did yesterday, so I definitely don't remember what I did 80 years ago.'"

So, he relied on what so often become the basis for such historical research, and which, he admits, have become "a lost, dying form": letters.

BISSINGER: These guys had a paper trail... The letters were simple, they were beautiful, they were homespun. You could feel their sense of loss; you could feel how much they missed home; you could feel how much they missed their fiancées. And there was a kind of gentle intimacy and beauty to them.

And then, you take the letters, and it's like any reporting: "What can I draw a string on here? How can I enhance it?" You look at a ton of articles, you look at film, you look at everything you possibly can, and interview other people – although there weren't that many, because they were so young when they died. You just interview as many people as you can, and keep drawing that string, and then you make the decision. "All right, I got enough."

Over time, a story took shape that homed in on four of the game's participants: John McLaughry, who was an All-American as a player at Brown University; Dave Schreiner, a future College Football Hall of Famer from Wisconsin; Bob Bauman, Schreiner's Badger teammate; and Tony Butkovich, who led the nation in rushing in his year at Purdue.

Hopefully, if you see this film, you are going to feel like you are in it.

Part of the choice to focus on these four was the drama in their stories – it will come as no surprise, watching the movie, that not all of them make it home from the war. But it was also "a matter of access."

"John McLaughry was a big star at Brown... His family, who I contacted, had kept everything – everything. Every letter, every report card, everything John had done in his life."

BISSINGER: Bauman was very lucky. I didn't get letters from Bauman until the last six months. I had written the book and his family said, "You know what? We have a foot locker from Bob we have never opened." This is his niece. "We've never opened it." It was his uniform, there were hundreds of letters, there were game balls... That's one of the delicious moments of reporting. You don't expect it, you have no idea, and they call and they say, "Well, by the way, you may be interested, we got hundreds of letters." What? Are you kidding me? I'm dying for that!

Both Berg and Bissinger admit it took a little time to crack the dense book's transition to film. But, eventually, Berg latched onto a story about the loss of innocence in war and a beautiful, fleeting moment when that innocence was recaptured.

Berg's vision for The Mosquito Bowl was "to make something that feels immersive... meaning hopefully, if you see this film, you are going to feel like you are in it." One unexpected source of inspiration in defining this approach? Gaspar Noé's Climax.

BERG: I can't recommend that film, but I will recommend that film if you're up for a challenge. It's a very intense movie, but it's experiential. I wanted to hit at that level. And as part of that, let's do it real.

Let's get real sets. Let's use real bombs, real flamethrowers, as safely as we could. Let's shoot 360 degrees, all that sort of stuff. And we were able to make things feel pretty visceral by doing that.

The impact of The Mosquito Bowl's practical, immersive approach to filming is felt from the very first combat sequence, which also happens to be one of the war's most traumatic. Our four protagonists have arrived in the Pacific and are preparing for their first taste of battle on Tarawa Atoll; they wonder to each other whether several hours of bombardment from US ships will have even left them anyone to fight. But as they approach to make their landing, their Higgins boat runs aground on a shallow reef, still a good distance from shore.

They barely have the chance to realize they've become sitting ducks before enemy fire comes raining down on them.

BERG: These guys have not had that much training, but they have been trained. They think they know what's going to happen. They think they're going to make the beach and fight, and they think that the air superiority and the bombardment from the battleships has softened the enemy. And from the moment it starts, they hit the reefs and everything goes to hell. That, for me, was certainly one of the moments that really pierced me when I read the book.

BISSINGER: I've read a lot about Tarawa. I can tell you, that is depicted [in the movie] to a tee. It is totally accurate. They knew the tide might not be high enough, but they let these kids go out anyway in these boats, and they became sitting ducks. They got hung up on the coral. All of a sudden, they're jumping off these boats. They got their rifles over their heads, because they don't want to get [them] wet, and they're being strafed and mortared by Japanese who were dug into the beach. At least 500 men died, and it was one of, maybe the greatest bloodbath and greatest strategic error that the Americans made during World War II.

To give all that visceral violence the emotional anchor it needs requires the right actors to play the four leads, and at least one decision came naturally. "I think it was Bill Skarsgård first," Berg recalled, "just because I really liked him." He plays Bob Bauman as a tough but upbeat man whose transition from football field to war zone feels the most natural of the group. Though he wouldn't seek it out, he is a little more comfortable with killing, something Skarsgård lends a slightly unsettling quality.

Nicholas Galitzine, who plays John McLaughry, and Ray Nicholson, who plays Tony Butkovich, both came through the audition process. "I was seeing so many actors, and I saw Ray, and I saw Nick... and they both kind of popped for me." Galitzine brings a poise that sells McLaughry as an athlete-scholar, and as the one most inclined to see the poetry in the world, his feelings run closer to the surface. Tony Butkovich, meanwhile, flashes that Nicholson family smile, and it tells you all you need to know about how he came to earn the nickname Touchdown Tony.

Before either of them came on board, however, Berg knew he'd found his Dave Schreiner. He just couldn't tell Netflix yet.

BERG: Right around [the time I cast Bill Skarsgård], I went and saw Sunset Boulevard on Broadway, and I saw Tom Francis. And I went back the next night. I saw it twice. He was so good in it. But I couldn't really offer him the role, because nobody knew who he was. I have a bit of say in casting, but if I'm just telling my bosses at Netflix, "It's Tom Francis," and they're like, "Huh? Who?" I had to read him, but I kind of knew he'd be next...

To see this young kid stand up there and command the stage like he did, that kid has real star power. I mean, I think they all do, but Francis, anyone who's seen Sunset Boulevard knows, has got this sequence where he just walks out into Times Square singing – it's mind-blowing. He's a very, very confident man.

Francis' performance balances sturdiness and vulnerability. Bissinger described the real Schreiner as "a natural," saying that "if you wanted to invent an All-American, Dave Schreiner would be it," and this quality comes through on-screen. He has a strong moral center that makes him the kind of character others would naturally follow. But he's also plagued by doubt, which Francis allows to peek through in very affecting ways.

The Mosquito Bowl cast also features a couple of notable cameos. NFL fans may recognize Pat McAfee, the former punter turned sports analyst, as the primary drill instructor yelling at our heroes as they train on Parris Island. He deflates a football with a bayonet, and even gets to recite the Rifleman's Creed.

Right there alongside him, though? Buzz Bissinger.

BISSINGER: Of course, Pete being who he is, I get to the set, and he says, "What are you doing here?" I say, "Pete, well, I wrote the book, and I'm observing, and I think you know that." He says, "No, get to costume, get to wardrobe! What are you doing?" I said, "Pete, why?" He said, "You're playing a marine drill sergeant." I said, "All right, fine."

I get to costume, they cut my hair, they fit me in an outfit. It was very easy for me to do, because all you have to do is tell people to shut the f**k up. That's all I said. And I was so good, I made the cut. That's one of the proudest moments of my life.

BERG: He stole the scene from Pat. We had to tone him down.

BERG: Once Buzz got going, he started barking at a level of intensity that McAfee couldn't keep up with.

Peter Berg also appears much later in the film, as a commanding officer on Guadalcanal who addresses the men in very frank, chilling terms. That small part was intended for Yellowstone franchise boss Taylor Sheridan, who was going to do it until "he realized how far of a flight it was from Texas to the Gold Coast." Berg was his own second choice, but he has no regrets about playing the role. He explained to SR that he believes acting in his films actually makes him a better filmmaker.

BERG: For me, acting in a film, I always try to give myself a little part, and I just like, five, ten years down the road, looking back and seeing, "Oh wow, I remember what I looked like and what I was feeling..." And the other thing, for me as a director, is I started off as an actor, and I haven't really acted in a long time substantially. And a director can forget or not know what the experience of acting is. And it's a uniquely weird job. It's stressful, and it can bring up insecurities, and you don't really feel like you have a lot of agency...

And as a director, sometimes I forget that, and I just might not be paying enough attention to a specific actor if they're struggling, or they want a little extra attention. Playing a part, and going to set as an actor, and going to the little trailer – which is basically a prison cell that you sit in, waiting for them to bring you into hair and makeup – going through that process humbles me, and reminds me of what I'm asking of the actors, because I forget it sometimes. So, I think it actually makes me more empathetic and probably a better director. My actors would maybe disagree with that, but I think it's true.

Not everything that happens in The Mosquito Bowl exactly mirrors history. Take the game itself: In real life, the two teams of Marines played to a scoreless tie. Staying true to that would've been tantamount to cinematic malpractice.

In approaching the adaptation, Berg made the distinction between 'fact' and 'truth.' Some facts were "critical" – where these men died, for example – and it was important that the movie maintain them. "Then I had to bring them together in ways that [were] not necessarily accurate to how they really all came together," he explained. "I had to condense timelines. They were in different battles, and I had to condense it and put them in one, often, certainly with Tarawa." Or, as he put it, "I changed some of the facts, but I kept the truth."

...you will never understand what these kids went through until you see this film.

Throughout, he trusted Bissinger to be his guiding light.

BERG: There's a line of credibility if you're going to say this is based on a true story. And I know that Buzz is going to be my audience, and he's got a real nose for this kind of thing, and he's going to be protective. I would send him pages and I would talk to him about it – and he jokes and says, "Well, if you're the writer of a book, and you agree to a movie, you got to take the money and shut the f**k up."

There's a little truth to that, but there's not, because the truth is also he would tell me if he thought I was crossing a line or doing something that was offensive or fundamentally violating the authenticity of what he's done. He'd tell me. He wouldn't be able to keep his mouth shut.

BISSINGER: I thought what Pete did – and I see this a lot in the film, having seen it now several times – is he took a basis in fact, and then he would have to mold it in a certain direction, because he's got a vision. He's the director. But I think a lot of it was intact. He even put a parrot into it, which I was shocked, because there's a little scene involving a parrot. Watching it was amazing.

Once creative license had its way, the throughline linking every scene was the unique way that football and war intersected for these young men. The movie's ideas emerge from how these two things spark against each other. According to Bissinger, this, too, is a truth extracted from the facts.

BISSINGER: Football played a curious role... The Navy saved college football because the Navy believed in football as the single best source of combat training for officers. What does it teach you? It teaches you the values that we talk about all the time. It teaches you discipline. It teaches you work ethic. It teaches you how to play when you're hurt. It teaches you about teamwork. It teaches you about realizing your dreams. So, it had a place in World War II.

And of course, the Mosquito Bowl was this unbelievable, bizarre, surreal, serendipitous, incredible football game that was really played on the island of Guadalcanal between not just those four guys, but some of the best college players in the country.

Of the 65 who played, 20 were drafted or would be drafted by the pros. There were seven captains. There were three All-Americans. The best receiver in the country was at the Mosquito Bowl. The best sophomore running back was at the Mosquito Bowl. You had talent. They would've beaten, if you put them together, these regiments, NFL teams. And so there was that moment of football.

But this is not a football book. This is a book about kids who play the game, who love the game, who are getting a ton of exposure, and whether they like it or not, they're going to war. This book is about one thing: war. It's sanitized all the time. War is about murder, war is about death, war is about brutality, and you will never understand what these kids went through until you see this film.

Like the book, The Mosquito Bowl is first and foremost about (thoroughly unsanitized) war. The characters are dragged through some of the worst that humanity has to offer, and the audience right along with them. But as much as the movie catches many of Bissinger's observations about how war and football may be complementary, Berg also uses football as shorthand for everything war is not.

The film opens with a quote from Herbert Hoover: "Older men declare war. But it is youth that must fight and die, and it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs." As much as football may prepare someone for the demands of being a soldier, it is also a game that emphasizes the youth of these men on screen. And, paradoxically, it is also inextricably tied to the futures that these talented players could have had. It's both the innocence and the potential that war costs its participants, all wrapped up in one.

For Berg, the Mosquito Bowl itself is the one moment this all shines through. In the historical record, it may be just one blip on the road to the Battle of Okinawa, which serves as this film's heartrending climax. But it's also this story's reason for being.

"It was the heart and soul of the book," Berg said, "even though it was a small moment, it was a powerful moment. It's what made it all kind of click for me, that you introduce trauma, you go deeper, you go deeper, you go deeper, you know you're headed for real trauma, Okinawa, and there's this moment of respite.

"This moment where these kids just get to be happy, as Buzz says, and just be kids and play."

#3382. ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner

Queer yearning (and suffering) is all the rage this fall season, especially among the Best International Feature Oscar contenders, from “La Bola Negra” to “Rose” and “Coward.” Lukas Dhont‘s Belgian Oscar entry follows two World War I soldiers (Cannes Best Actor winners Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne) in a furtive, forbidden romance that can only flourish in and around the trenches — necessitating their desire to stay in battle. Watch the latest trailer, an IndieWire exclusive, below.

The sweeping World War I romance comes from the young Belgian filmmaker whose last film, Cannes winner “Close,” received a Best International Feature Oscar nomination. Related Stories 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’ Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer

Per MUBI, “Surrounded by brutality but bound by tenderness, two World War I soldiers find a fragile sanctuary of love and art amid the shadows of the Belgian trenches. ‘Coward’ asks a profound question for a generation sent to war: when the world demands violence, is walking away the truest act of bravery?”

More from IndieWire’s review: “Belgian filmmaker wrestles the tenderness and softness between soldiers from the brutality of the battlefield in his visually arresting if thematically by-the-book third feature, ‘Coward.’ Starring newcomers Valentin Campagne and Emmanuel Macchia as achingly beautiful soldiers of the Belgian front in World War I who fall in love and learn to discover that, in one of the most fascinatingly contradictory ideas of Dhont’s highly contradictory career, the violence of war is what both enables and protects their attraction, and allows them to be together at all.”

There’s more, as “in 1916, on the western front of World War I, the flamboyant Francis (Valentin Campagne) leads a not-so-merry band of rejects among his infantry, of soldiers whose job it is to entertain and raise the morale of their comrades. In this case, it’s forming a theater troupe of the soldiers in drag as they move from battle to battle, a role that’s become almost as instrumental in keeping spirits high as actual combat is to wearing them down. The withdrawn, ethereally beautiful Pierre (Emmanuel Macchia) becomes drawn into the world of the troupe, and he’s intrigued by the outré Francis’ ostentatious theatricality, and how comfortable he is in dresses and makeup. … Through an attraction that’s only allowed to flower because of and in context of their closeness to each other on Francis’ performances, he and Pierre become secret lovers.”

Watch the new trailer, an IndieWire exclusive, below. MUBI opens the film in theaters throughout the United States and Canada on December 25 (that’s Christmas Day).

#3381. This iPad Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Yes, Apple participates in Cyber Monday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy, Amazon, and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

#3380. Oobah Butler Wants to Expose the World’s Stupidest Industries, but They Get Worse Faster Than He Can Plan His Stunts

It’s a spectacular time to be a grifter. Basic truths keep getting harder for people to agree on, marketing is more dependent on hackable algorithms than traditional gatekeepers, and it seems like everyone is willing to uncritically listen to anyone offering them a shortcut. As Oobah Butler puts it in the first episode of his new HBO series “Scams for a Better Tomorrow,” we’re living through a “gold rush of bullshit.”

If that’s the case, Butler is a prospector who hits a paystreak everywhere he looks. After beginning his career as a musician, the British performance artist has devoted much of his past decade to the art of the scam. In 2017, he made headlines for creating a TripAdvisor profile for a nonexistent restaurant that briefly became the highest-rated eatery in London. His penchant for scams has only grown since then, culminating in “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow.” The five-episode, “Nathan for You”-esque series sees him grift his way to the top of some of the slimiest industries on the planet including wellness supplements, wine, and dating apps with an approach that blurs the line between satire and how-to guides. Related Stories Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

When we spoke over Zoom, it was the first time I had ever interviewed a scammer. I naturally had to ask Butler if that was his preferred term (he had no problem with it), and how he would characterize his own unorthodox line of work.

“I think it sits somewhere between gonzo journalism and comedy. And I think we’re in a moment, in a culture, that’s just so rife with inauthenticity and scamming,” Butler said, explaining that just watching run-of-the-mill advertisements on a streaming service are enough to convince you that we live in an insane world. “One in three [ads] are AI now. And I don’t know why, that stuck in my mind recently where I was like, ‘Wow, these aren’t real people trying to sell me a product. They’re like prompts in a machine.’ So it’s an interesting line of work, but I think it feels very now, to be honest.”

The series should be essential viewing for anyone who either wants to laugh at the state of our seemingly elite spaces or just wants to make a quick buck in a dirty industry. Episodes illustrate how ecosystems of influencers and online ratings can be easily manipulated in pursuit of accomplishing ludicrous goals, like turning an undrinkable bottle of smoke tainted cabernet into one of Napa’s highest-rated wines of the year or marketing a skincare product as “endorsed by Cameron Diaz” because a random Hispanic guy was willing to slap his name on it for $50.

It’s a funny enough premise, but Oobah and his small team (which included frequent Safdie collaborator Ronald Bronstein) found that their best laid plans left them insufficiently prepared for the greed and stupidity that they’d encounter in the real world. The first episode begins with a scheme to market a new skin serum that’s allegedly made from the tears of small children. They thought that ridiculous idea could serve as the climax of an episode, but they soon found that the grifters they encountered had little issue with the idea — some of them even thought they could make money on it with the right tear-shaped bottle. The joke remained in the show, but it had to be reduced to a starting point before the episode devolved into crazier plans.

“We had a tip from a journalist that dermatologists can be full of shit and that they often can take money in exchange for recommendations. So we set up a lab where I had these kid actors with goggles on with tubes coming off them, and it was like we were milking the kids for the tears or whatever. We were like, ‘Right, we’re going to invite this dermatologist down here,’ a high-end Manhattan dermatologist, and we expected the dermatologist to laugh us out of the room,” he said. “What we couldn’t plan for doing that stunt is that the dermatologist would be like, ‘Awesome. Yeah, this is cool. Yeah, all right, interesting product. Maybe we could keep on working together, but I expect an endorsement fee.’ And I’m like, ‘Oh, you don’t give a fucking shit. You don’t care.'”

The incident cuts to the central problem of a show like this: it’s hard for satire to keep up with a world that only seems to get crazier every day. But Butler is not shying away from the challenge. He works quickly (the show began shooting this spring and wrapped in October before premiering on November 22), and is willing to change his plans whenever it turns out that a sincere actor has beaten him to one of his comedic scams. He already has plenty of ideas for a hypothetical Season 2, including taking on the recent trend of hotels and vacation rentals using AI-generated images that look nothing like their actual rooms. But the one thing he can count on is that the bullshit gold rush is not going to end any time soon.

“It’s hard to satirize something that’s so insane and fucked up,” he said. “That’s why in the first episode, we go and make a new product because it felt like the children’s tears thing wasn’t crazy enough. You know what I mean? So I literally go and make a human meat supplement, a lab-grown human meat supplement, and we go to this lab in Austin, we take stem cells from my stomach, we grow it over months and we create this thing. Because the actual reason we did that was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think children’s tears is scary because influencers would promote that.’ So I suppose that the crazier things get, the crazier the satire has to be able for it to be effective.”

“Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow” airs Sunday nights on HBO at 11 p.m. ET/PT before streaming on HBO Max.
