#3378. 8 Perfect Sci-Fi Books With No Bad Characters

Great character writing is not strictly essential to all speculative fiction, but there's a good reason why it's the backbone of most of history's greatest science fiction books. Though worldbuilding, pacing, stakes, and themes are just as crucial for a piece of science fiction to be truly legendary—and, at best, downright perfect—great characters are also important, which is probably why several of the best sci-fi books ever are also among the sci-fi books with the most interesting characters.

There are many things that can make a sci-fi book character great, but the key element is that readers are able to deeply connect with them regardless of whether they're an alien, a cyborg, or a space-faring human. Throughout the years, eight particularly noteworthy sci-fi books that happen to not have a single bad character, on top of being absolutely faultless themselves.

The mere high-concept pitch for Tamsyn Muir's Gideon the Ninth is so deliciously absurd that it makes it instantly clear why this is such an irresistibly fun modern classic: lesbian necromancers exploring a haunted palace in space for just under 450 pages. It's an effortlessly genre-blending gem with elements of space horror, Gothic suspense, and dark fantasy, making it one of the most purely entertaining and original science fantasy novels the world has seen in years.

Another big part of why Gideon the Ninth is one of the best science fantasy books since 1990 is the fact that the whole ensemble of characters is every bit as memorable as the plot. Gideon herself narrates the book with an irreverent voice that feels like a breath of fresh air for this genre. Muir also makes sure to constantly pair characters that may seem disparate on the surface, but this only results in a constant stream of fun moments that make every character come alive perfectly.

Canadian writers' contributions to science fiction sometimes go underappreciated, which should absolutely not happen when praising the brilliance of Emily St. John Mandel's Station Eleven. Before it was turned into one of the most genuinely perfect miniseries of the last couple of decades, it was one of the most perfect post-apocalyptic novels of the 21st century, breaking away from the genre's usual tropes by celebrating the beauty of life and art rather than dwelling on the grimness of its dystopian premise.

Where a lot of post-apocalyptic fiction tends to flatten its characters into cheap stereotypes, Mandel is careful to never do that. Instead, Station Eleven is built on a large ensemble of characters who, though flawed, feel beautifully human and fully realized. No matter how small their role, every character is given a chance to show off their complexity and moral nuances, including a primary antagonist with so many deep layers that he never feels like any kind of villainous caricature.

When it comes to speculative fiction authors, few have ever been as groundbreaking or influential as Ursula K. Le Guin; and when it comes to the sci-fi works of such legends, few have ever been as revolutionary as The Dispossessed. The winner of all three of the Hugo, Nebula, and Locus Awards for Best Novel, this game-changing masterpiece strikes a faultless balance between utopian and dystopian sci-fi, exploring how no sociopolitical system is ever truly finished or beyond any need for change.

It's one of the best soft sci-fi books of all time, written with the utmost intelligence throughout—that intelligence extending to the phenomenal character writing. It would have been abundantly easy for any lesser writer to allow their characters to become mouthpieces for political or philosophical ideologies, but Le Guin never does that. Instead, her characters are vulnerable, psychologically complex, and deeply human. Shevek is one of Le Guin's most enrapturing protagonists, and the rest of the ensemble is just as important in elevating the book's thought-provoking themes.

The 20th century saw the publication of many a great book set on Mars, but remarkably few of them were better than Kim Stanley Robinson's Red Mars. This landmark in modern hard sci-fi writing is a must-read for anyone who loves the genre, setting a new standard for realistic Mars colonization narratives and sociologically complex world-building. It won the Nebula Award and launched the equally successful Mars trilogy; but as great as its sequels are, it's Red Mars that stands out as the best.

On top of the nearly unmatched scientific rigor, the jaw-dropping sense of scale, and the central philosophical question of whether humanity should prioritize terraforming Mars for humanity's benefit or preserving its natural life, you get some of the most human and believable character writing that hard sci-fi literature has ever seen. Every character seems to embody a different attitude toward the core ethical question that fuels the narrative's sense of momentum, but those attitudes feel deeply ingrained into their arcs rather than making them feel like cardboard-cutout archetypes.

Leviathan Wakes and the Expanse series that it sparked were born as a pitch for a massively multiplayer online role-playing game, which then evolved into a tabletop RPG campaign. The journey culminated when Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck, writing under the pen name of James S. A. Corey, finally put pen to paper and turned the concept into Leviathan Wakes, which ended up being one of the greatest space opera books of all time. Grounded, tonally nuanced, and full of geopolitical complexity, it's a perfect masterpiece through and through.

It should come as no surprise that a book which was born out of an RPG campaign has characters with very distinct skills and personalities, clear motivations, and ensemble chemistry that feels remarkably organic. The rest of the Expanse series also has excellent character writing, but Leviathan Wakes perhaps deserves the most credit for being the one to introduce this incredibly memorable cast. As perfect narrative foils for each other, Jim and Joe are the best dual protagonists that a hard sci-fi space opera could possibly ask for.

There are many who would still praise Frank Herbert's Dune as the single greatest and most influential sci-fi novel of the 20th century. Regardless of superlatives, there's practically no denying that as far as space opera books go, it doesn't get much more perfect than this. Thematically layered and narratively momentous, this cautionary tale against the dangers of charismatic leaders and religious fanaticism has only kept getting better with age.

It's one of the most essential sci-fi books to read before kicking the bucket, and that's in no small measure thanks to how timeless and memorable the character writing is. Paul is such a complex and layered protagonist that many people back in the '60s (and today) misunderstood him and saw him as a tragic hero rather than a cautionary figure. Then you get villains like Baron Harkonnen and Feyd-Rautha, and secondary characters like Chani and the Lady Jessica, all amounting to one of the most iconic ensemble casts in the history of sci-fi literature.

If Dan Simmons' Hyperion is one of the most amazing sci-fi books ever written—and it is— it's in no small measure thanks to the character writing. However, by no means is that the only strength that this masterpiece has going for it. Borrowing the structure of Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales, Simmons gave birth to not only the origin of the incredible Hyperion Cantos series, but also to one of the most ambitious and masterfully genre-blending sci-fi novels ever written.

Indeed, Hyperion is an absolute masterclass in virtually every way that matters in sci-fi writing, which inevitably brings the conversation back to its many fascinating characters. Because each pilgrim in this story gets roughly a novella-length backstory dedicated to their psychology and motivations, the characters become the book's entire plot. No one here is a clear-cut hero, which generates friction between characters that likewise results in the book's most engrossing and unforgettable moments of narrative momentum.

Who, if not Ursula K. Le Guin, could possibly be said to be responsible for not only one, but two of the sci-fi books with the most perfect character writing in the genre's history? When it comes to asking what the most perfect sci-fi novel Le Guin ever wrote could be, it's not actually much of a debate at all: Fans tend to agree that it has to be The Left Hand of Darkness. One of the best sci-fi books written since Dune, The Left Hand of Darkness won the Hugo and Nebula Awards thanks to how it completely revolutionized how sci-fi authors wrote first contact stories.

The novel mainly relies on two of the greatest and most fascinating characters that sci-fi literature has ever produced: Genly, a well-meaning but subtly prejudiced Starfleet captain whose journey of learning how to be humble and open-minded is the emotional heart of The Left Hand of Darkness; and Estraven, a disgraced prime minister whose dynamic with Genly is so enrapturing that it's reason enough for any sci-fi fan to immediately pick up this absolutely perfect novel. Add to that an ensemble of great side characters as the cherry on top, and you get one of the best sci-fi books in history.

#3377. GTA 6 PC Port Officially Shut Down By Rockstar

Grand Theft Auto 6 is smashing records in sales, but it's currently doing so without any assistance from the PC market. Despite the juggernaut status of the game's launch, it's only available to those with a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S, leaving plenty of fans anticipating the game to wait until a PC release that is assumed to be on the way.

Some fans who aren't willing to wait, however, have attempted to take things into their own hands first. The biggest project to bring GTA 6 to PC was a recompilation effort called "Leonida," but its development is officially over, in part due to GTA 6 Rockstar Games stepping in.

On X, "Leonida" creator NotRexed announced that they were stepping away from the project thanks to issues that they "can't control." The announcement followed its disappearance from GitHub on the previous day. In a follow-up tweet, they clarified that Rockstar taking down their server was one part of the reason for quitting, but that they already had too much going on as a teenager "without having middle aged men yell and complain to you on discord."

Leonida was intended to provide a framework for running GTA 6 on PC, natively running the code thanks to the similarity of Xbox and PC architecture, reimplementing Xbox system software, and translating graphics computing programs. While it was still in an early stage of development, making it impossible to actually play the game on PC at the moment, it was considered a promising foundation for playability in the future.

Leonida's shutdown likely won't be the last anyone sees of GTA 6 recompilation projects, as the wait for a PC port will leave plenty of fans with time on their hands. Recomps have become increasingly common in recent months thanks to the accessibility of pulling them off with the use of AI "vibe coding," although there have also been recent projects made entirely manually with a higher standard of all-human coding.

For those who are able to play GTA 6 on consoles, it's proven to be a technical masterpiece. The game pushes the PS5 and Xbox Series X to their limits, but it manages to retain visual clarity, using traditional scaling solutions to bump up an internal 1440p resolution to 4K output rather than relying on a sub-HD resolution and a scaling solution like DLSS for blurrier results. Xbox Series S takes a hit, unsurprisingly, but the results are still impressive considering the system's weaknesses.

In terms of performance, the biggest appeal of a PC port would be the potential for 60 FPS performance, which is currently inaccessible even on the PS5 Pro. A port will also open the door to modding, which, in traditional Grand Theft Auto fashion, will doubtless take the game in some wild new directions. Hopefully, Rockstar Games will introduce the world to an official PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 in 2026, along with the anticipated release of a new online mode.

#3376. The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’

Rita Coburn‘s “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is an extraordinary documentary about an extraordinary man, a film that spans nearly 100 years in two hours, yet never feels rushed or superficial. In her storytelling, Coburn shares with her subject a talent for distilling complex ideas and expressing them with force and clarity; the result is a movie that fully honors the breadth and depth of Du Bois’ achievements as a groundbreaking Black writer, historian, and activist.

One of Coburn’s most potent tools in this regard is the music by composer Kathryn Bostic, who previously collaborated with the director on “Marian Anderson: The Whole World in Her Hands.” Bostic incorporates a wide array of styles and influences in her score, which references the various types of music Du Bois encountered and appreciated as a Black intellectual but isn’t beholden to them; as evocative of Bach and American folk music as it is of 19th-century spirituals and Asian motifs, it’s the sonic equivalent of Du Bois’ literary works. Related Stories ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’

The scope of the project required Bostic to come at the material from multiple angles and perspectives. “Rita and I talked about what types of touchstones we needed to define the narrative musically,” Bostic told IndieWire. “There was the regional touchstone, the era-specific touchstone, the interior emotional aspects that we wanted to heighten with music. Then there’s always the discovery process as you begin to create.”

For Bostic, that discovery process is one of the most exciting aspects of film composing. While she had a number of reference points as she began work on the score, she soon found herself following intuition to take them in different directions than initially intended. “There’s always what I call the hands-on-the-clay moment,” Bostic said. “You have your list, and you have your frame of reference, but the process is fluid.”

According to Coburn, Bostic’s ability to bring a historical perspective to her scores made her an ideal collaborator for the film. “Kathryn pulled from the region of Great Barrington [where Du Bois was born] as well as New York in that time period, and then what was happening with the African-American community that Du Bois was entering,” Coburn said. “There wasn’t gospel then, so you were looking at a small group of Black people going to the churches there in New England. What were they listening to, and therefore what was he listening to?”

Bostic drew on the music of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a Black a capella ensemble that inspired Du Bois, but then moved in a completely different direction to explore his time in Berlin, when he encountered and fell in love with classical music. She also incorporated Wolof music from Senegal and the Gambia in collaboration with Coburn’s daughter, who studied classical music and worked in the music department on “Rebel with a Cause.”

“She found a Senegalese professor online who worked with her so she could sing the Wolof,” Coburn said. “Kathryn and I agreed that we had to put the Wolof in the film because it connects Du Bois to his Ghanaian roots. But we had to find it, and we wanted it to be as authentic as possible.”

For Bostic, the challenge was taking an audience from 2026 and presenting the music in a way that would recreate the way in which Du Bois experienced it over a hundred years earlier. “There’s the historic arc of the times, as well as what he’s experiencing emotionally,” Bostic said. In the places where her score was informed by spirituals and the work of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, the composer tried to tie the emotional subtext to the context in which she knew Du Bois was consuming the music.

“When he went to Fisk University, his mother had recently died,” Bostic said. “So that music was a wellspring for his grieving, and I think that depth of sorrow and the catharsis that resulted from that sorrow inspired the sort of deep self-reflection that became such a deep part of who he was. That self-reflection led to a basic decency and humanity, and even now I think of him as being light years ahead of people in the way he embodied justice. I want to shine a light on that.”

Coburn felt a similar sense of purpose, especially since the more she dug into Du Bois’ life the more she realized how relevant his insights were to America in 2026. “He speaks to this current time,” Coburn said, adding that the importance of Du Bois’ work gave her own work a sense of urgency and responsibility. “I knew that it might be 20 or 30 years before we get another Du Bois documentary. I hope not, but I looked at his life and knew that I had to do the best job that I could. We did everything we could for Du Bois because we felt he had done everything he could for us.”

The greatness of “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is that it brings the viewer into Du Bois’ perspective as his world view continues to expand over a 95-year life, and the music is a major part of that subjectivity.

“Kathryn understands that music is a character in any documentary, and her music embodies the character of W.E.B. Du Bois,” Coburn said. “ In the music, we had to grow with him. We had to expand with him. We had to see that his love of Rembrandt and his understanding of classical music, of music that came from an Asian culture, that all of that was important to him. We were catching up with him, and he was driving us.”

“W.E.B. DuBois: Rebel with a Cause” is currently streaming on the PBS app and website.

#3375. If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar shows) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

The Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

#3374. Watch the ‘Project Hail Mary’ VFX Supervisor Explain Why Having Puppeteers on Set Was Worth All the Extra Work

The making of “Project Hail Mary” was a miracle on par with the outer space rescue mission that Ryan Gosling is tasked with pulling off. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s bestselling novel manages to be epic without ever losing its intimacy, as Gosling traverses the galaxy and saves the world with only a very lovable rock acting alongside him. The final product was a complicated blend of practical effects, on-set puppetry, and a healthy dose of VFX magic.

Incorporating so many production elements creates more work for all involved. The puppetry team lead by James Ortiz had to fit into very small spaces, which frequently meant they showed up in the frames. Visual Effects Production Supervisor Mag Sarnowska and her team were tasked with removing all of the puppeteers. But as she explained during the VFX panel at IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables, it was a small price to pay for the way it enhanced Gosling’s acting performance. Related Stories The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’ ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner

“It was so good to have James and his puppeteers, which we called Rocketeers,” Sarnowska said. “It was great to have them there, but it did not work out sometimes. Our sets were really, really tiny. Having five people there to puppet Rocky was hard sometimes. But to everyone’s point, having something there in the frame was so helpful, especially for Ryan to act to. The eyeline? That’s a real thing. Even though our Rocky didn’t have eyes, a person’s brain makes it easier to figure out where the eyes would be just by having that constant relation between Rocky and Ryan.”

Sarnowska — who will share the Innovation Award at the IndieWire Honors with Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, and Paul Lambert — explained that having a real reference point for VFX sequences is what ultimately makes the most effects-heavy sequences feel real.

“In Ryan’s space, he has to be in the xenonite glass, so having reflections, adding the glass, it was a lot of work,” she said. “But having that real thing, having that reference, even if we had to replace it, that was so important. Because we knew what Rocky would look like.”

Of all days on the broadcast television schedule, Super Bowl Sunday has always held a coveted status. The big game itself is always a cultural moment that routinely draws in hundreds of millions of viewers to see the culmination of the NFL season live, with all the bells and whistles attached. However, it's also a crucial day for whatever series gets to air in the immediate aftermath and benefit from the colossal lead-in. Networks in the past have typically used the spot for new series they've felt confident about and special episodes of ratings darlings, with everything from The Office to The Late Show with Stephen Colbert and Survivor airing afterward. This year, with ABC hosting the festivities, it will be the latter.

After being held for the midseason for the first time since its debut in 2024, High Potential will be making up for lost time with a special Season 3 episode right after the Super Bowl on February 14. The Kaitlin Olson-led crime drama will regularly air on Tuesdays, starting on January 5, but the bonus time slot will be utilized to give the series a massive spotlight and allow new showrunners and Scream 8 writers Nora and Lilla Zuckerman to get creative with Morgan Gillory and the LAPD. Taking a page from the last time they hosted the big game in 2006, with Grey's Anatomy getting the lead-in, ABC will be airing the first piece of a two-part storyline with a cliffhanger that will be resolved on February 16. Plot details are unknown at this time.

High Potential was about a slam dunk to earn the coveted lead-in for the network's first Super Bowl in a decade. It finished the 2025/2026 broadcast season pacing all broadcast television programs in the key demographic of adults 18-49 and ranking third in overall 35-day multiplatform viewing with over 16.01 million tuning in on average. That came after it went toe-to-toe with CBS' ever-popular Tracker for the title of most-watched network series of 2025. Enough viewers have fallen in love with Morgan and her unconventional crime-solving ways to make the series a suitably buzzy pick to follow up the biggest sporting event of the year in the U.S.

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

Created by Drew Goddard, High Potential has seen Morgan rise from an LAPD cleaner with an IQ of 160 to a trusted civilian consultant of the Major Crimes Division, using her intellect to solve the crimes that vex the police. Her unique approach makes her the surprisingly perfect partner for the by-the-books detective Karadec (Daniel Sunjata), whose own methods tend to run up against the sleuth's. Season 3 will pick up after a climactic finale that saw Captain Wagner (Steve Howey) left on death's door by a gunshot and Morgan's missing husband, Roman, potentially visit their daughter's art show under the cloak of secrecy. As such, Howey will be sitting out this season, but Javicia Leslie joins Olson and Sunjata among the returning cast, alongside Deniz Akdeniz, Amirah J, Matthew Lamb, and Judy Reyes rounding out the bunch.

High Potential Season 3 premieres on January 5. Stay tuned here at Collider

#3372. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

#3369. 10 TV Shows Recommended By Oprah

Few figures have shaped the television industry as much as Oprah Winfrey. Throughout her decades-long career, the legendary talk show host has become one of entertainment's most influential voices, using her platform to introduce audiences to compelling stories and talented performers. Although she is best known for The Oprah Winfrey Show, her influence extends far beyond the programs she has hosted herself.

Oprah's recommendations have long carried considerable weight, particularly in literature. Her celebrated book club has introduced millions of readers to new authors and unforgettable stories, demonstrating her ability to influence what audiences consume. However, her appreciation for powerful storytelling isn't limited to the written word.

Television has undergone a remarkable transformation throughout Oprah's career, evolving from traditional sitcoms and procedural dramas into an industry increasingly defined by ambitious narratives and morally complex characters. Her recommendations reflect that evolution, encompassing groundbreaking comedies, acclaimed dramas, and historical series that have helped redefine what television can accomplish.

From beloved classics that challenged societal expectations to modern productions that pushed the boundaries of serialized storytelling, the television shows recommended by Oprah represent some of the medium's most celebrated achievements. While these programs differ considerably in tone and subject matter, each offers something that has resonated with audiences and contributed to television's enduring cultural impact.

Few sitcoms have developed quite the same cult following as Arrested Development. Created by Mitchell Hurwitz, the series follows Michael Bluth (Jason Bateman) as he attempts to hold his dysfunctional family together after his father is arrested for financial crimes. Unfortunately, the Bluth family's selfishness and questionable decision-making continually undermine Michael's attempts to restore some semblance of normalcy.

What distinguishes Arrested Development from traditional sitcoms is its unconventional approach to comedy. Its intricate running jokes, clever callbacks, and layered storytelling reward attentive viewers, with seemingly insignificant moments often becoming important several episodes later.

Although the series struggled to attract a large audience during its original Fox run, its popularity grew considerably afterward, eventually prompting Netflix to revive it. Right from Arrested Development's masterful pilot episode, its distinctive comedic style has helped establish the series as one of television's most influential modern sitcoms.

Created by David Simon, HBO's The Wire offers an uncompromising examination of Baltimore through the interconnected lives of police officers, drug dealers, politicians, and ordinary citizens. Rather than following the familiar structure of a conventional crime procedural, the series explores how deeply entrenched institutional failures affect nearly every aspect of the city.

Each of The Wire's five seasons examines a different institution, gradually expanding its perspective beyond law enforcement to include organized labor, education, politics, and journalism. This ambitious approach allows the series to examine systemic problems without reducing them to individual villains or straightforward solutions.

The best TV shows of all time will be debated forever, but there are clear contenders. These are the very best TV shows of all time, ranked.

The Wire​​​​​​'s morally complex characters and commitment to realism distinguish it from other crime dramas, while its social commentary remains relevant long after its conclusion. Although it never became a major ratings phenomenon, The Wire has earned widespread recognition as one of the greatest television dramas ever made.

Breaking Bad transformed what initially seemed like a straightforward crime drama into one of television's most compelling character studies. Created by Vince Gilligan, the AMC series follows Walter White (Bryan Cranston), a high school chemistry teacher who begins manufacturing methamphetamine after receiving a terminal cancer diagnosis. What starts as an attempt to provide financial security for his family gradually becomes something far more sinister.

Walter White's transformation from an apparently unassuming teacher into the ruthless Heisenberg remains one of television's most memorable character arcs. His increasingly destructive decisions also demonstrate how easily audiences can become invested in morally reprehensible protagonists.

Alongside Aaron Paul's performance as Jesse Pinkman, the show's meticulous storytelling and escalating tension helped redefine expectations for serialized television dramas. Its enduring popularity eventually led to the acclaimed prequel Better Call Saul, further expanding the franchise's legacy.

Adapted from George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire novels, HBO's Game of Thrones became a worldwide phenomenon through its ambitious world-building and willingness to challenge traditional fantasy conventions. Set primarily in the fictional continents of Westeros and Essos, the series follows rival families competing for political power while an ancient supernatural threat emerges beyond the northern border.

Rather than relying on straightforward distinctions between heroes and villains, Game of Thrones develops an expansive ensemble of morally complicated characters whose competing ambitions frequently lead to devastating consequences. The show's shocking character deaths and elaborate political maneuvering helped make the series appointment television, generating widespread discussion between episodes.

Although Game of Thrones' eighth and final season remains controversial, its extraordinary production values, cultural influence, and ability to bring epic fantasy to mainstream television have secured its place in entertainment history.

Larry David built upon his success as the co-creator of Seinfeld with HBO's Curb Your Enthusiasm, a comedy that takes the awkwardness of everyday social interactions to absurd extremes. David stars as a fictionalized version of himself, whose inability to tolerate minor inconveniences or follow unspoken social conventions regularly creates elaborate misunderstandings.

Unlike traditional scripted sitcoms, Curb Your Enthusiasm relies heavily on improvisation, allowing its performers to develop conversations around predetermined story outlines. This approach gives the series a distinctive sense of spontaneity while making its increasingly ridiculous situations feel surprisingly believable.

Throughout Curb Your Enthusiasm's 12 seasons, the comedy also attracted numerous celebrity guest stars, frequently portraying exaggerated versions of themselves. David's willingness to expose the absurdities of social etiquette, even when his character is so often clearly in the wrong, helped establish Curb Your Enthusiasm as a defining achievement in modern television comedy.

Created by Matthew Weiner, AMC's Mad Men transports audiences into the competitive world of advertising during the 1960s. Mad Men primarily follows Don Draper (Jon Hamm), a talented but deeply troubled ad executive whose carefully constructed professional identity conceals a complicated personal history.

Don Draper may have had 3 wives in Mad Men, but that didn't stop Sterling Cooper's creative director from having affairs with 18 women in the series.

Through Don and his colleagues, the show explores the era's changing social expectations and cultural attitudes. Although Mad Men unfolds against the backdrop of a glamorous advertising industry, its greatest strength lies in its examination of deeply flawed characters navigating personal and professional challenges.

The series particularly excels in its portrayal of women confronting workplace discrimination and shifting gender roles, with Peggy Olson and Joan Holloway emerging as two of its most compelling characters. Its meticulous period details and sophisticated writing helped establish Mad Men as a defining example of prestige television.

Few period dramas have achieved the widespread popularity of Downton Abbey. Created by Julian Fellowes, the British series follows the aristocratic Crawley family and their household staff as they navigate the dramatic social changes of early 20th-century England.

Beginning shortly after the sinking of the Titanic, the story explores how historical events gradually transform the lives of those living at the fictional Yorkshire estate. Although the series features the lavish costumes and elaborate settings associated with traditional period dramas, its appeal extends beyond its impressive production design.

By exploring the relationships between the Crawleys and their servants, Downton Abbey examines class divisions alongside the personal struggles shared across social boundaries. Its combination of historical storytelling, family drama, and romance attracted an international audience, eventually inspiring multiple feature films that continued the beloved characters' stories beyond the original series.

Based on Piper Kerman's memoir and created by Jenji Kohan, Netflix's Orange Is the New Black follows Piper Chapman (Taylor Schilling), a privileged woman sentenced to prison for a crime committed years earlier. Initially centered on Piper's adjustment to life behind bars, the series gradually expands its focus to explore the experiences of an exceptionally diverse ensemble of incarcerated women.

Orange Is the New Black distinguishes itself by balancing dark comedy with serious examinations of systemic inequality. Its use of flashbacks provides valuable insight into the women's lives before incarceration, challenging audiences to reconsider their initial perceptions of individual characters.

The series also broke significant ground through its representation of LGBTQ+ characters and its exploration of issues affecting marginalized communities. As one of Netflix's earliest original successes, Orange Is the New Black helped demonstrate the potential of streaming platforms to produce culturally influential television.

HBO's The Sopranos fundamentally changed expectations for television drama when it premiered in 1999. Created by David Chase, the series follows New Jersey mob boss Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini), whose struggles with anxiety lead him to seek psychiatric treatment. Balancing the demands of organized crime with his complicated family relationships, Tony becomes an increasingly fascinating examination of power, masculinity, and moral corruption.

Rather than presenting its central character as a conventional hero, The Sopranos challenges audiences to sympathize with someone capable of extraordinary cruelty. Its psychological complexity and willingness to explore uncomfortable subjects helped popularize the morally ambiguous television antihero.

From The Wire to Breaking Bad to Mare of Easttown, TV audiences have been treated to all kinds of crime drama masterpieces over the years.

The series also demonstrated that television could deliver the same narrative sophistication traditionally associated with acclaimed cinema. Its influence remains evident in countless subsequent dramas, particularly those built around deeply flawed protagonists, making The Sopranos one of the most influential shows in television history.

Long before television became dominated by complicated antiheroes and serialized dramas, The Mary Tyler Moore Show was challenging expectations through its portrayal of an independent career woman. The universally loved sitcom stars Mary Tyler Moore as Mary Richards, a single woman who moves to Minneapolis and begins working as an associate producer at a local television station.

Rather than defining Mary primarily through her romantic relationships, the series emphasizes her professional ambitions, friendships, and personal independence. Premiering during a period of significant cultural change, The Mary Tyler Moore Show offered a groundbreaking depiction of a woman building a fulfilling life outside traditional expectations of marriage and motherhood.

Its talented ensemble and sophisticated humor also helped redefine the workplace sitcom, influencing generations of television comedies. More than five decades after its premiere, the show's progressive storytelling and enduring charm remain essential parts of its extraordinary legacy. Oprah Winfrey has frequently cited The Mary Tyler Moore Show as one of her personal favorites, saying the iconic sitcom is what inspired her to create her own TV show.

#3368. Why Black Friday and Cyber Monday Are Bad Days to Impulse Buy Electronics

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Browse our editors’ picks for a curated list of our favorite sales on laptops, fitness tech, appliances, and more.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a big "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Awards season will be making a stop in San Francisco on December 7 for the annual SFFILM Awards Night, honoring four artists who’ve made an impact this year.

John Turturro, acclaimed this year for his performance in “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” will receive the Maria Manetti Shrem Award for Acting, named for the Italian-American philanthropist. (Turturro will also receive IndieWire Honors recognition on December 3.) Carrie Coon, who made a big-screen splash this year in “The Liberation,” will receive the Katie & Todd Traina Award for Acting. “Carrie, Guitarricadelafuente, Peter, and John each bring a distinct sensibility and an uncommon command of their craft to the screen this season,” said Jessie Fairbanks, SFFILM’s director of programming. “We selected this group because they represent the range of talent and creative perspectives that make cinema so compelling, and their work speaks to the thoughtful, nuanced, and often unexpected films that make a season memorable. #3364. How to Cancel Your Amazon Prime Membership After Black Friday and Cyber Monday

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

One of Amazon’s biggest sales of the year, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, is set to start Nov. 27, but many early deals are already rolling in. To take advantage of everything the sale has to offer, you’re going to need to be a Prime Member. If you sign up for an Amazon Prime account to take advantage of the sale but decide you don’t want to pay for an ongoing membership, you’ll need to cancel your subscription before the end of your free trial.

You can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

#3363. 5 'Tulsa King' Actors Who Also Appeared in 'The Sopranos'

Sylvester Stallone's Dwight “The General” Manfredi may be a fish out of water in Oklahoma, but Taylor Sheridan's popular series Tulsa King is a homecoming for anyone who spent the late ’90s and 2000s in the company of one of HBO's best series, The Sopranos. The key to this show's immense success is, without a doubt, co-creator and showrunner Terence Winter, who was an original writer and executive producer on The Sopranos. In 2010, he went on to create another hit for HBO, Boardwalk Empire, bringing some Soprano alumni along with him.

Similar to Boardwalk Empire, Winter has also brought several stars from The Sopranos into the fold of Tulsa King, including Max Casella, who played Benny Fazio, and Annabella Sciorra, who fans remember for her role as Tony's stunning but troubled gumad, Gloria Trillo. While there's still a chance for more familiar faces to show up in Paramount+'s latest success, this list highlights five stars from Tulsa King (almost no one remembers #5) who also appeared in The Sopranos!

Known for starring alongside Neil Patrick Harris on the hit sitcom Doogie Howser, M.D., Max Casella made his first appearance in the Season 1 premiere of Tulsa King as Armand "Manny" Truisi, an ex-soldier for the Invernizzi crime family who fled New York and settled down to start a quiet life with his wife and kids in Tulsa, where he started working for Margaret Devereaux (Dana Delany) at Fennario Ranch. After squashing the past with Manfredi, Truisi joined his crew, but his broken marriage and financial desperation set him on a course of betrayal and self-destruction that ended with him taking his own life at the end of Season 3.

Before he was the Oklahoma Kid, Casella starred in The Sopranos as Benny Fazio, a loyal soldier who worked his way up in the Soprano/DiMeo crime family. Casella made his first appearance in Season 3, Episode 3, "Fortunate Son," as Fazio, who shows up after being released from county jail and is now working for his friend and recently made man, Christopher Moltisanti (Michael Imperioli). Out of the 20-plus episodes he appeared in, Casella's character is mostly remembered by fans for his hilarious tiff with Artie Bucco (John Ventimiglia) in Season 6, which landed him in hot water with Tony.

In Season 1, Episode 4, "Visitation Place," fans meet Manfredi's younger sister, Joanne Manfredi, played by Annabella Sciorra, who had previously starred alongside Stallone in the 1997 crime thriller Cop Land, which also stars other Soprano alumni including Edie Falco, John Ventimiglia, and Tony Sirico. Throughout the show, Joanne has since become a major player in her brother's extensive operation and is one of the few people who can keep Manfredi in check and level-headed. While Joanne is not a woman to be messed with, she has nothing on Sciorra's character from The Sopranos, Gloria Trillo.

Sciorra made her debut in Season 3, Episode 8, "He Is Risen," as the strong-willed and fiery Gloria Trillo, who meets Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini) in Dr. Melfi's (Lorraine Bracco) office and eventually becomes his gumad, but their passionate affair is short-lived after Tony sees her true, toxic nature. Despite her trauma and baggage, fans remember Gloria and Tony's relationship as one of the most revealing and intense dynamics in the entire series, which also led to Tony having a significant breakthrough about his relationship with his mother, Livia (Nancy Marchand). Even though her time on the show was brief, Sciorra delivered an unforgettable performance, and I know I speak for every fan when I say it's nice to see her back in the spotlight on Tulsa King.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

In Season 3 of Tulsa King, Manfredi has his work cut out for him as he goes head-to-head with a powerful Dixie Mafia leader and boss of a moonshine empire, Jeremiah Dunmire, who is played by the underappreciated Robert Patrick. Widely known for his role as T-1000 in James Cameron's Terminator 2: Judgment Day, Patrick gives an intense and merciless performance in Tulsa King and is easily one of the series' best characters, but before he was setting house fires and terrorizing the people of Tulsa, Patrick appeared on The Sopranos as the degenerate gambler, Davey Scatino.

In Season 2, Episode 6, "The Happy Wanderer," fans meet Scatino, the owner of a local sporting goods store who has known Tony and Artie since they were kids. When word reaches Scatino that Tony is taking over Uncle Junior's (Dominic Chianese) executive card game, he weasels his way into the game (unaware that he was manipulated by Tony), but he makes the grave mistake of thinking that his past with the mobster and the friendship between their kids would get him a pass on the massive debt he accumulated. Even though Dunmire and Scatino couldn't be more different, Patrick executes both roles with incredible ease, which essentially showcases his underrated range and versatility as a performer.

Chris Caldovino stars in Tulsa King as Dennis "Goodie" Carangi, a former high-ranking member of the Invernizzi crime family who joined Manfredi's crew as a consigliere and de facto second-in-command after the General severed ties with the Family. Caldovino delivers a powerhouse performance as Goodie, who is known for his unwavering loyalty, cheeky humor, and quick wit, and has since become a recurring fan favorite. Before he became the General's right-hand man, Caldovino briefly appeared in The Sopranos as Phil Leotardo's (Frank Vincent) younger brother, Billy Leotardo.

In Season 5, Episode 3, "Where's Johnny?," viewers meet Billy Leotardo, who is an associate of the Lupertazzi crime family as well as his older brother's partner in crime. As tensions continue to rise between New York families, Tony's cousin, Tony Blundetto (Steve Buscemi), seeks revenge after his mentor, Angelo Garepe (Joe Santos), is murdered by the Leotardo brothers in retaliation, and ends up killing Billy, essentially dragging Tony and his crew into the chaos. Caldovino appeared in a total of nine episodes of The Sopranos, and even though it would have been nice if he stuck around a little longer, it's great to see him front and center in Tulsa King.

Best known for his breakout role as the charming Charles "Lucky" Luciano in Boardwalk Empire, Vincent Piazza stars in Tulsa King as Vince Antonacci, a former capo turned consigliere in the Invernizzi crime family who initially views Manfredi as a threat to his territory after being released from prison and is a driving force behind sending the General out West. Since establishing himself in Tulsa, Antonacci has landed himself on The General's bad side and has been a constant pain in his ass, operating as the middleman between Manfredi and New York's Quiet Ray Renzetti (James Russo). The majority of people might think Piazza followed Winter from Boardwalk Empire, but only die-hard Sopranos fans know that isn't the case.

Piazza made his debut in Season 6 of The Sopranos as Hernan O'Brien, a wealthy and reckless friend of AJ Soprano's (Robert Iller) who gets the mob boss's son involved in the party scene and plenty of trouble. He made his first appearance in Season 6, Episode 8, "Johnny Cakes," appearing in a total of three episodes, with Season 6, Episode 13, "Soprano Home Movies," being his last. In fairness, Piazza was pretty young when he appeared in The Sopranos, and since he only briefly appeared in several episodes, it's easy to understand how some might forget (or not even recognize) that he was in the groundbreaking series.

#3362. ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

A very successful “values-based entertainment” company that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul. Related Stories Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie

With “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

Not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

Let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production company Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and shows that amplify light.”)

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

Every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

Later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel company, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

Of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the company’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

The holy grail of Derek Jeter cards has finally surfaced on the auction block ... and it's arguably the most coveted card ever featuring The Captain!
