Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

Are you ready for a rude reminder about the fragility of time? December is nearly here. Impossibly, we’re already heading into the final stretch of 2026, though at least the best streaming services are helping to soothe that calendar shock with a fresh slate of new movies and TV shows. And HBO Max, in particular, has a stacked lineup with which to spend your final weeks of the year.

Things kick off on December 1 with a fist-pumping throwback as an iconic, multi-decade boxing franchise — spanning from Sylvester Stallone’s 1976 classic to its modern spinoffs — steps into the ring. Elsewhere on the film front, a provocative comedic thriller led by the winning duo of Olivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman makes its streaming debut on December 4, before an acclaimed sci-fi horror sequel lands later in the month to keep things spooky.

Over on the TV side, the platform is capping things off on Christmas Day with a polarizing new series adaptation that kicks off a fresh era for a massive wizarding franchise. From nostalgic knockouts to broomstick-flying drama, here’s a guide to everything new on HBO Max in December 2026.

One of the most talked-about new movies of the so-called "awards season" thus far has been "I Play Rocky," an underdog biopic starring Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone during the tumultuous production of his iconic boxing flick "Rocky," which famously went on to win the Oscar for Best Picture. But before you tune into that new bio-drama, why not go back to where it all started with a big "Rocky" movie marathon?

Helpfully, HBO Max isn't just bringing back the 1976 original — which is celebrating its big 50th anniversary this year and centers on a small-time Philadelphia boxer (Stallone) who gets a once-in-a-lifetime chance to face the world heavyweight champion in the ring — but all nine films in the "Rocky" franchise beginning on December 1. That includes the "Rocky" sequels “Rocky II” (1979), “Rocky III” (1982), “Rocky IV” (1985), “Rocky V” (1990) and “Rocky Balboa” (2006), as well as the Michael B. Jordan-led "Creed" spinoff trilogy comprising “Creed” (2015), “Creed II” (2018) and “Creed III” (2023).

That should keep you busy until New Year's, right?

Stream "Rocky" on HBO Max starting December 1

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Few Hollywood stars had a 2026 like Olivia Wilde, who directed arguably the year's best comedy, "The Invite," and also pops up opposite Pedro Pascal in the cellist dramedy "Behemoth!" and alongside Cooper Hoffman in this Gregg Araki-directed erotic comedy.

In "I Want Your Sex," Wilde plays renowned artist and provocateur Erika Tracy, who takes fresh-faced twentysomething Elliot Bell (Hoffman) as her assistant and sexual muse. As their arrangement begins to blur professional and personal lines, Elliot is pulled into a world of sexuality, obsession, power, betrayal and murder.

Along with Wilde and Hoffman, the star-studded cast includes Charli XCX, Mason Gooding, Chase Sui Wonders, Johnny Knoxville, Margaret Cho and Daveed Diggs.

Stream "I Want Your Sex" on HBO Max starting December 4

One of the most anticipated TV titles of the year has also been its most controversial, drawing backlash over J.K. Rowling's involvement, casting choices, and, most odd of all, children's teeth. Regardless, plenty of HBO viewers will undoubtedly be tuning into another year at the Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, with a new set of fresh faces playing some of modern-day literature's most iconic characters.

The eight-episode series will follow pretty much the same plotline as the first "Harry Potter" book and subsequent film, with Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger, Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley, John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall, and Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape.

#3277. Don Was Pays Tribute to Bobby Weir by Reimagining a Classic Dead Album

When Blues for Allah was recorded by the Grateful Dead at Bob Weir’s home studio in 1975, the band had been looking far to the east, incorporating North African melodies and instrumentation to accompany lyricist Robert Hunter’s conceptual imagery. Some 50 years later, noted producer and Blue Note Records president Don Was only had to travel to the midwest to interpret the songs of the seminal album (fan favorites “The Music Never Stopped,” “Help on the Way/Slipknot,” and “Franklin’s Tower” among them), linking with jazz trumpeter and composer Terence Blanchard for a one-off show for his curated Paradise Jazz Series at the Detroit Symphony Orchestra.

The idea of revisiting Blues for Allah was prompted by Laina Cohen, the Golden Road Festival founder who suggested Was and his band perform the album at the 2025 gathering in Buford, Georgia, to celebrate the LP’s golden anniversary. After years of playing with Bobby Weir and the Wolf Bros, Was was the ideal candidate to reinterpret the album with elements of blues and jazz and a Detroit swing. The only problem was he didn’t have his own band. So, Was set forth to form one.

“I called people who I knew were awesome musicians, but I also knew we all grew up listening to the same radio stations and playing in the same bars and playing for the same tough audiences,” he says. “They’re open and receptive and as enthusiastic as you can be.” Dubbed “the Pan Detroit-Ensemble,”  the group, featuring saxophonist and Blue Note Records artist Dave McMurray, keyboardist Luis Resto, trombonist Vincent Chandler, and vocalist Steffanie Christi’an, proved to be the perfect vehicle.

Still, confronting the odd time signatures and elaborate instrumentation of the album left Was stumped. “‘King Solomon’s Marbles’ was one that really required some work,” he says. “I always thought it was just a jam, and I thought the reason it didn’t get played was because it was just something that happened once. As we got into it, I realized there’s actually a very specific and clearly delineated structure to the song.”  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Was worried the fan base wouldn’t respond positively. “I was [concerned] that we’d gone too far for some fans, that it was sacred ground, but it wasn’t the case at all,” he says. “No one ever had a problem with adapting it because they could tell it was done in service to the song.”

“Crazy Fingers” was another tough song for Was and his band. “We used to play that in Wolf Bros, and it’s sort of reggae, sort of Irving Berlin. It’s a very weird feeling, and if you don’t get it exactly right, it falls flat,” he says. “It didn’t come naturally to nine people from Detroit. So what did come naturally was to turn it into a six-eight thing like Otis Redding’s ‘Dreams to Remember.’”

Was started working on this project before Weir’s death last January, and played some of the music for his longtime friend and bandmate.  “He dug it. And my guess is that had he survived a year, he’d have come out and played some,” Was says. “He heard a little rehearsal thing, and he’d seen YouTube stuff of  ‘Shakedown Street’ and ‘Loser‘” in our very first shows, and he loved it. He was very proactive about making sure that the music would outlive all of us, and he really welcomed that.”

As fate would have it, the first date of Was’s Blues for Allah tour fell on the day Weir died. “We were in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and I had to go out and tell them. I didn’t feel like doing it, but I remembered Bobby talking a lot about the night Jerry died, and they were in New Hampshire, and they went out and played. He said, ‘You bring comfort to people by playing good music for them.’ So we played the songs, and then I went out and sat with the audience for a while, and we talked about Bobby, and everyone had stories to tell. I found it incredibly comforting. For all the subsequent shows, it became a place to go and grieve.”  Related Content Grateful Dead's Official Blanket, Towel, and Poncho Collab Is 20% Off for Black Friday The Restless Storytelling at the Heart of the Grateful Dead Bill Kreutzmann Plans ‘A Very Grateful Thanksgiving’ in Hawaii My Morning Jacket Connect the Grateful Dead Dots in Faithful San Francisco Residency

Was and the band toured throughout the year and on Nov. 20 released their own live version of Blues for Allah.  Trending Stories Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Snapshots From Miley’s Wedding: ‘Beautiful’ to See Family ‘United by Love’ U2 Will Bring Their ‘Greatest Show on Earth’ Stadium Tour to North America in 2027 Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Anthem Singer Apologizes for ‘O Canada’ Flub at Leafs-Islanders Game

Bobby’s presence is still felt. As Was shares, “The weird thing is that I don’t feel like he’s gone. He’s ubiquitous, man. You turn on SiriusXM radio anytime, and he’s on, and the music’s everywhere, and we’re out playing the music. When he talked about Jerry, he would say that he could feel like Jerry was kind of on his shoulder. I thought he was being hyperbolic, but I liked the image of it. It’s actually how I feel. I kind of got him in there when I’m playing, because I’m used to playing these songs with him, and playing in the Wolf Bros changed the way I played in a big way.”

And like the Dead, the musical experimentation continues: Was’s next project is the Dead’s prog epic Terrapin Station, coinciding with the album’s 50th anniversary in 2027.

#3276. 10 'Find Hub' Hacks Every Android User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Google's Find Hub app isn't just for tracking your lost smartphone. Over the past year, Google has consistently added features to manage your belongings, share your location with loved ones, and locate lost devices. Find Hub can now notify you when you've left your device or your tracker behind. Plus, you can use Gemini to remember where you left items, even without a tracker attached. Behind the scenes, there are even more hidden settings and features to help track your devices and make it easier to retrieve them in case they are stolen or misplaced. If you use Find Hub, you need to know about these 10 hacks.

This month, Google finally added Left Behind notifications to Android trackers—but you have to enable the feature manually. AirTags users should be familiar with this feature already. When you leave your tracker or device behind, and exit the location range, you’ll receive a notification that you left without your item. You need to enable this feature on a per-device basis. Go to Find Hub and select a device. Tap the settings gear icon next to the device's name, and enable Notify when left behind. While you’re here, go to Add location to add familiar locations where you don’t want to get a notification (like your home or workspace). Otherwise, Find Hub may spam you with left behind alerts.

There’s a hidden feature in the Find Hub app that helps you keep track of things without actually using a Bluetooth tracker. You can simply ask Gemini to remember where you put things, and it will show up in the Find Hub app. To use it, pull up Gemini and say something like, “Remember in Find Hub that the passport is in the downstairs wardrobe,” or “I’ve kept the spare car keys behind the garage door.”

You can then ask Gemini, “Where did I keep my passport?” and it will tell you. If you change the location of an item, just ask Gemini to update it for you. When you go to the Remembered tab, you’ll see the location of all remembered items. You can also add items manually here using the Add button.

Some Android smartphones can remain findable for several hours after they've been switched off or their batteries have run out. If you’re using a supported device (like the latest Pixel series smartphone), you can use a hardware feature to track the location using Google’s mesh network, relying on nearby devices (similar to how Android tags work).

To make sure this feature is enabled, go to Find Hub, and tap Find your offline devices. Here, make sure that either With network in busy places only or With network everywhere is selected.

If you’re using a tracker in your car, luggage, or on your keys, you might want to share location access with your spouse or family members. Find Hub has a feature called "Share Ownership" that lets you share the tracker details with up to 10 people. Only the location of your tracker is shared, not your personal device.

To set it up, go to Find Hub, and choose the tracker or accessory that you want to share. Tap the Share Ownership button and follow the on-screen instructions to share the invite link via a messaging app or using Quick Share. Once the recipient taps Accept, you’ll get a notification. Go to the device settings in Find Hub and tap the Confirm button to enable location sharing.

You can quickly share your live location with your friends or loved ones using Google Messages. Open a conversation, tap the Attachment icon, and choose Real-time location. Set the duration and tap Send.

If you don’t like using the Messages app, you can do so directly from Find Hub. Go to the People tab at the bottom of the screen, and tap the Plus icon. Choose the duration and select a contact to share the location with, then tap the Get Link button to copy the link. You can then share it via any messaging app of your choice.

You might have a Find Hub tracker in your luggage to help keep tabs on your bags. But you don't have to be the only one privy to its location. If your airline loses that luggage, you can temporarily share its location with your airline to help you retrieve it. This is an official feature, too: Google partnered with multiple airlines to make this data sharing easier. From the Find Hub, choose your tracker. Tap the Share Item Location button, and then tap Share Item Location again. Copy the generated web link and share it with your airline using the app or support page. The link will automatically expire in seven days, so you don't have to worry about your airline continuing to monitor your luggage's location long after your flight.

Find Hub uses a mesh network of supported Android devices to securely locate your lost device or tag. But by default, it waits until multiple Android devices detect the location of the lost device. This works well if you've lost the device in crowded areas, but it can increase your wait time if you lose it somewhere remote. Luckily, there is a hidden setting that triggers location sharing even if a single device reports its location. Go to Settings > Google > All services > Find Hub > Find your offline devices and select With network everywhere instead of With network in busy places only.

If you’ve lost your smartphone, you don’t need to rush to a computer or a website to track it. Borrow someone’s Android smartphone and head into their Find Hub. Tap Sign in as guest and sign in with your Google account associated with your device, then find and select your device in the account. If requested, enter the PIN that you’ve previously set up. You can now track the device’s location, get directions to the device, or play a sound to help track the device if it’s nearby. If the device is truly lost, you can use the Mark as Lost feature to remotely lock your device.

Map-based tracking is helpful in getting to the general vicinity of your lost device. But your smartphone or tracker is hidden; finding it may require precision tracking. Many newer trackers like the Pixel Tag come with an ultra-wideband chip that helps you find the exact location of the tracker, given you are nearby. This also works on Pixel smartphones (Pixel 8 Pro series and above) and Samsung Galaxy devices (S21 and above, Plus and Ultra models only).

When using this feature, make sure you have Bluetooth enabled on your smartphone, then open Find Hub. Choose your tracker, and tap Find Nearby. Follow the on-screen instructions to locate the nearby device. You can also tap Play Sound to make the location process easier.

If you think your Android smartphone is lost or stolen, don’t rush to erase all data. While a remote factory reset is great for protecting your data, it also removes the device from your account. It’s best to try to get the device back. Two-factor authentication (or a passkey) on your Google account, along with a biometric lock on your smartphone, will protect the data itself.

Go to the Find Hub website, or use Find Hub on someone else’s phone in guest mode. Choose your device, and instead of Factory Reset, choose Mark as Lost. Here, you’ll see an option to enter a message. Type an alternative contact number, and a message to help recover the device.

#3274. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3273. The Wallet-Sized Xteink X4 Pro Is Lifehacker's E-Reader Gift of the Year, and It's on Sale for Black Friday

I've read more than 30 books in the past year, all of them on an e-reader with a screen roughly the size of a credit card. If you think that sounds untenable, I say: Don't knock it 'til you've tried it. Once you're immersed in a book, you'll find the size doesn't matter, and the convenience of being able to slip it into any pocket and forget it's there means you need never be without it.

Right now, the Xteink X4 Pro, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far—and Lifehacker's pick for the 2026 E-Reader Gift of the Year—is on its best sale yet for Black Friday: When ordered directly from Xteink, you'll save 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84. This is the cheapest e-reader with a light and a touchscreen that you can buy right now, and it's well worth the money.

The X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4 Classic, it adds two big upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. As a result, it costs a bit more, but you can pick one at a $15 discount right now. (Even at full retail, the X4 Pro is $50 cheaper than the entry-level Kindle after its recent price increase—and even considering the Kindle's current Black Friday discount).

Meanwhile, if you're a reader who prioritizes the crispest text over conveniences like a front light, the 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic and the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 are about $30 less during Amazon's own Black Friday sale.

As much as I love them, these minuscule e-readers aren't for everyone. Some may indeed find the screen too small (though if you've ever read a book on a phone, the experience is similar). Then there's the fact that they can't load your existing libraries of Kindle books; you'll need to source copies of e-books lacking Digital Rights Management (DRM) software. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

#3272. Tidal Is the First Streaming Service to Ban AI Music

Tidal has announced an ambitious plan to ban all music wholly generated by artificial intelligence.

On Dec. 9, the streaming service will start rejecting uploads of all music made with AI, and removing any that are currently on the platform. Tidal head Robert Anderson stated that all AI tracks will be gone by the beginning of 2027.

The new policy will apply only to music made completely with AI tools like Suno, Lyria, and Udio. Tidal will continue to allow tracks made with the assistance of AI tools, “but not the sole outputs” of them.

As Anderson noted on X, this decision makes Tidal the first digital streaming platform to ban AI music, and he pointedly encouraged others in the industry to “follow suit.” The move comes after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing AI-generated tracks over the summer.

The proliferation of AI music on streaming platforms has caused numerous headaches for artists and labels over the past few years. While much of it goes unnoticed — Tidal estimated 96 percent of the AI songs it’s already flagged have garnered zero streams over the last 90 days — tracks that do catch on can divert streams and royalties from working artists.

There are also fraud concerns, whether it’s bots streaming AI-generated music, or scammers uploading AI tracks under the names of actual artists. Tidal said it’s already taken down over 65,000 such tracks “flagged for suspected artist-name impersonation.

“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” Tidal said in its statement.

Speaking to the scale of the AI music problem, Tidal estimated that there are 27 to 29 million AI tracks on its platform now (about six percent of its total catalog). Additionally, the company said 43 percent of all uploads from the past 90 days were flagged as wholly AI-generated. Anderson said the platform expects to reject anywhere between 80,000 to 85,000 songs per day once the new policy goes into effect.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

While Tidal’s reject-and-remove policy is a novel step in the effort to combat AI slop, effective enforcement could pose some challenges. Earlier this year, DistroKid, the largest music distribution platform by volume, accidentally removed a bunch of real music, made by real artists, while doing mass takedowns in response to a copyright infringement lawsuit filed by Universal Music Group. (DistroKid apologized for the accidental takedowns, and has denied UMG’s accusations.)

Tidal has, however, at least been able to test out its detection tools thanks to its efforts to flag and demonetize AI music over the past few months. A rep for Tidal did not return a request for comment about the success rate of its detection tools, but streamer’s tech partner, Ircam Amplify, boasts 99 percent accuracy and false positives under one percent.  Trending Stories Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Snapshots From Miley’s Wedding: ‘Beautiful’ to See Family ‘United by Love’ U2 Will Bring Their ‘Greatest Show on Earth’ Stadium Tour to North America in 2027 Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Anthem Singer Apologizes for ‘O Canada’ Flub at Leafs-Islanders Game

Along with using these tools to determine whether a song is made with AI, Tidal said would ban distributors from “delivering these tracks to us” and would “reject delivers if their metadata says they were generated solely using AI tools.”

Tidal said its AI policy “was designed to provide a great experience for listeners, while protecting the authenticity and livelihoods of artists and rightsholders. Tidal will always fight for artists to get paid more. Everything in this update comes back to that. If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for, or copied by someone pretending to be you. We’ll keep sharing what we find and we’ll keep acting on it.”

We want to hear it. Send us a tip using our anonymous form.

#3271. iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing with developers and public beta users. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 …

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left, making it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also brings a new face unlock feature to iPhone Duo. This is not full-fledged Face ID. Instead, Apple is using the front-facing camera on the iPhone Duo’s outer display to recognize you, then unlock the device. It doesn’t work for things like Apple Pay and passwords.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

Finally, iOS 27.3 includes a new option in the Settings app to have your iPhone Duo lock when closed. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold it, rather than transition content from the inner display to the outer display.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 also introduces usage limits on select Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features. The limits apply to things like:

You can unlock higher usage limits with an eligible iCloud+ plan, starting at $2.99 per month. If you hit your usage limit, basic Siri requests will still work. That includes things like setting timers and alarms.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:

iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

There are two key changes to the Apple TV app in iOS 27.3. First, the update introduces video podcasts in the TV app. You can now watch your favorite video podcasts in the TV app, and sync your playback progress between the TV app and the Podcasts app.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds vertical video to the TV app. The app now includes a new “Explore Clip Collections” section where you can browse clips from Apple TV content in a TikTok-style design.

Here are a few other changes in iOS 27.3:

What are your favorite new features in iOS 27.3? Have you spotted any other changes in the update? Let us know down in the comments.

Both systems have a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio, producing three parts filtered water for each part sent to the drain. If you’re shopping for a reverse osmosis water filter, countertop models make it possible to upgrade without changing the plumbing beneath your sink. Renters, apartment residents, and anyone who wants water ready for tea at the touch of a button may prefer a countertop RO system.

#3268. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

#3267. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

If you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.)

If you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

For about $30 more than the X4 Classic, you can upgrade to the Xteink X4 Pro, which happens to be Lifehacker's e-reader Gift of the Year pick. It offers all the perks of the other Xteink devices, with two critical quality-of-life upgrades: A touchscreen for easier navigation, and a temperature-adjustable front light so you can read it in a dark room. (Less obviously, it also has a slightly faster processor that makes the whole thing feel a little snappier.) Right now, the X4 Pro is at its lowest price ever when ordered directly from Xteink: $84, or around 15% off the usual $99 price.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3266. Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal

Sonny Bono’s widow, Mary Bono, is appealing her defeat in a four-year royalties war with Cher, arguing in a brief filed Monday that a federal judge erred last year in ruling that Cher’s 1978 divorce agreement with Sonny Bono took precedence over federal copyright law. Mary Bono contends that the federal Copyright Act entitles her and Sonny’s children to reclaim the 50 percent share of his songwriting royalties awarded to Cher in the divorce.

In his ruling last year, U.S. District Court Judge John Kronstadt found that Cher’s marital settlement agreement entitled her to a 50 percent share of Sonny’s composition royalties, rather than an interest in the copyrights themselves. As such, he found that her claim was protected by state contract law and not subject to the termination rules of the Copyright Act.

In the divorce settlement, Sonny awarded Cher the 50 percent cut of his composition royalties for hit songs including “I Got You Babe” and “The Beat Goes On.” Cher also got a 50 percent share of the musical recordings they made together. In court filings, Cher’s lawyers said Mary had “secretly” begun diverting Cher’s royalties to herself and Sonny’s other heirs after using the termination provisions of the Copyright Act. Cher sued, and the court determined her grant was untouchable.

In the new 33-page appellate brief obtained by Rolling Stone, Mary and her lawyers sharply criticize the ruling. They argue the lower court “struggled with the concept that copyright terminations preempted Sonny’s right to contract freely and bargain away his heirs’ rights.” They say copyright termination “trumps the common law’s freedom to contract.”

“Sonny could not have alienated Mary’s right, as his widow, to the post-termination copyright interests when he entered into the MSA in 1978. Despite any language to the contrary in the MSA, all of the reverted rights, including the right to receive royalties, belong to the heirs,” the brief, filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, states. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“The District Court focused extensively on family law questions and, in particular, spousal support, even though the parties agree that the MSA is a contract like any other,” the filing reads. “This unfortunately led the District Court to err by failing to acknowledge that the federal Copyright Act preempts state law on the issue of copyright terminations.”

Attempts to reach Cher’s lead lawyer on the lawsuit were not immediately successful Tuesday. The lawyer, Peter J. Anderson, previously argued in court that the Copyright Act was clear, and that by the time Sonny and Cher signed their divorce settlement in August of 1978, they were “sophisticated people” represented by “sophisticated lawyers.”

He said Sonny and Cher knew during negotiations that “I Got You Babe” and “Bang Bang” were big hits. “They knew this. They also knew that the 1976 Copyright Act was in effect and that on January 1, 1978, it had a termination right. So, when they said Cher gets 50 percent of all royalties from all sources, that includes under the replacement publishing agreements when they terminate the initial publishing agreements,” Anderson argued to the court. “These songs were already tested by the marketplace. These sophisticated people already knew about termination rights.” Trending Stories Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Snapshots From Miley’s Wedding: ‘Beautiful’ to See Family ‘United by Love’ U2 Will Bring Their ‘Greatest Show on Earth’ Stadium Tour to North America in 2027 Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Anthem Singer Apologizes for ‘O Canada’ Flub at Leafs-Islanders Game

Cher’s side will have a chance to respond before the appeals court issues any ruling.

Cher, 80, rose to fame alongside Sonny in the 1960s before building a decades-long solo career that brought her Grammy, Oscar, and Emmy wins. Sonny died in a skiing accident in 1998, leaving Mary in charge of his estate. His music publishing grants became eligible for termination beginning in 2018.

Apple TV (now $6.99/month for limited time) has just unveiled the return of one of its most popular series: Presumed Innocent. Here’s the release date and first trailer.

Presumed Innocent, the legal thriller starring Jake Gyllenhaal, was a big hit for Apple when it aired in 2024. Though it was originally conceived as a limited series, Apple gave it a surprise renewal for season 2.

The sophomore season of “Presumed Innocent” is based on “Dissection of a Murder,” the debut legal thriller novel by Jo Murray, who also serves as a co-executive producer. Up-and-coming defense attorney Lelia Reynolds (Brosnahan) faces off against her district attorney husband (Rhys) in a murder case that threatens to destroy both their careers and their marriage.

You can watch Presumed Innocent season 1 on Apple TV. The eight-episode first season tells the story of “the horrific murder that upends the Chicago Prosecuting Attorney’s office when one of its own is suspected of a crime.”

Apple has started making a habit of renewing shows that were originally intended as limited series.

#3263. If You Loved 'The Diplomat,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary). Kate Wyler (Keri Russel) is a mess in many ways, and almost every major character is at emotional, moral, or intellectual loose ends. This would all be in good fun if these characters weren’t also some of the most powerful people in the world—presidents, prime ministers, and the high-level politicians and diplomats that serve them.

If you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom during what could be described as tumultuous times (and you’ve watched all our series streamalikes), allow me to suggest the one perfect movie that delivers similar vibes: 2009's In the Loop.

Released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos. It’s actually a spinoff from a British TV series from the same co-writer/director, Armando Iannucci: The Thick of It. Many of the characters and situations are based on some of the people actually running the U.K., but you don’t need to be familiar with the show or the real history to enjoy the heck out of this movie. That goes double for Peter Capaldi’s absolutely ferocious performance as Malcolm Tucker, a man so creative with his profanity that many of his F-bombs will live rent-free in your head for years to come.

When a not-so-bright minister in the U.K. government (played by Tom Hollander) makes some dimwitted remarks that threaten to blow up Britain's carefully crafted diplomatic messaging around potential military adventures in the Middle East, Tucker (the prime minister's director of communications) has to tamp down the growing chaos that results. This eventually requires a contingent of British diplomats and officials to head to Washington, where they are quickly overwhelmed by the superpower vibes they encounter.

It’s a more profane, faster-paced, and outright comedic story than The Diplomat, but it’s also easy to imagine most of the characters showing up on that show. The film also shares that same sense of controlled chaos that drives The Diplomat—the idea that a handful of tired, dedicated people are continuously racing around to prevent World War III even as dumber and more powerful people keep creating new crises. If Kate Wyler’s constant state of exhausted anxiety is your jam, you’ll love this movie. Stream In the Loop on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Want more cynical diplomats, secret plans, and international skulduggery with a side of personal emotional crises? Here are a few more movies fans of The Diplomat will love.

If you want a sense of what actual back-channel diplomacy is like, watch Ben Affleck’s Best Picture winner Argo, from 2012. Based on the remarkable true story of how six U.S. diplomats were rescued from Tehran during the Iran Hostage Crisis under cover of a fake sci-fi movie production, the film has the snappy energy and fast pace of The Diplomat combined with real-world danger. You can easily imagine Kate and Hal (Rufus Sewell) being part of the secret, off-the-books conversations that brought what’s known as the Canadian Caper into reality. Stream Argo on Paramount Plus or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite parts of The Diplomat are the schemes various players (mostly Kate and Hal) get up to in their efforts to shape world diplomacy and history to their liking, Wag the Dog is a good bet. When a sex scandal threatens to swing the Presidential election away from the incumbent, a spin doctor (Robert De Niro) wades in to save the day by convincing a top Hollywood producer (Dustin Hoffman) to “produce” a fake war in Albania to distract the American public. It’s equal parts funny, compelling, and depressingly instructive, and fans of the show will love the back-channel hijinks. Rent Wag the Dog on Prime Video.

One of the great things about The Diplomat is watching Kate Wyler, a smart and capable woman who generally knows more than anyone else in the room. If that’s the dynamic that grabs you, The Contender is the overlooked gem for you. When the vice president dies unexpectedly, the President (Jeff Bridges) nominates Senator Laine Hanson (Joan Allen) to take the post. A conservative senator (Gary Oldman) opposes her nomination and launches a smear campaign to derail her confirmation. There are dirty tricks and secret deals, and in the middle of it all, Allen’s terrific performance as a woman who refuses to back down in the face of sexist, unfair attacks. Stream The Contender on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Apple TV.

Nicole Kidman plays an interpreter at the United Nations, a woman who has a unique heritage and linguistic knowledge. When she overhears an assassination plot in an obscure dialect, she becomes embroiled in a dangerous game of espionage and high-stakes diplomacy as she races to prevent disaster (and keep herself alive). The Interpreter is a more serious and much more tense story, but it delves into the background work that makes the global system function, which puts it right in the sweet spot for fans of The Diplomat. Stream The Interpreter on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

This might not seem like a match at first glance—a comedic treatment of the power struggle that followed the death of Soviet Premier Josef Stalin in 1953—but it absolutely is. Making a farce out of the political wrangling among the members of the Central Committee, the film has the same spirit as The Diplomat, showing that the people in charge are a bunch of schemers, tricksters, dummies, and sociopaths. Watching them run around making deals and angling for advantage offers the same energy as the show. Plus, it’s just plain hilarious. Stream The Death of Stalin on Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3262. Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

“It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the company’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time …

Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

It’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.)

I’m a big fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, users should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy users at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, users had to wait until it “just worked.”

Apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an update, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

Another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

It’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech users may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

Is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.
